anchor_text: bequeathed me by will but poor a thousand crowns
summary: Orlando's father left him only a thousand crowns in his will, while his eldest brother Oliver inherits the estate outright. Under the law of primogeniture — the convention Orlando calls 'the courtesy of nations' — the oldest son inherited everything, and younger sons depended on whatever their father chose to set aside. A thousand crowns was a modest sum, not enough to sustain a gentleman.
detail: Primogeniture was the dominant inheritance rule in Elizabethan England for landed families: the estate passed whole to the eldest son to prevent its fragmentation. Younger sons had to make their own way through the church, law, military service, or marriage. The father's will also charges Oliver to educate Orlando well — the obligation Oliver ignores. The play's opening complaint is thus immediately recognizable to any audience member with younger brothers: the law is clear, but its spirit can be violated.

sources.name: Elizabethan inheritance law
sources.citation: W. Holdsworth, A History of English Law, vol. 3 (1923), pp. 185-190, on the common law rule of primogeniture for freehold land.

anchor_text: keeping for a gentleman of my birth that differs not from the stalling of an ox
summary: Orlando uses 'keeping' to mean maintaining or providing for a person (feeding, housing, clothing) as a master does for a dependent. He is pointing out that the way Oliver provides for him — just enough to stay alive without any education or refinement — is indistinguishable from how you would keep a farm animal in a stall. The insult is that Oliver cares no more for his brother than for his livestock.
detail: Both 'keeping' (providing for) and 'manage' (training horses in controlled movements, the discipline of horsemanship) are technical terms from equestrian culture that Orlando turns to bitter irony: he knows what proper breeding of a gentleman's horse involves — skilled riders hired at high cost — yet Oliver spends nothing on the education of his own blood. The contrast between the horses' 'manage' (training) and Orlando's complete absence of training is the scene's central grievance.

anchor_text: his countenance seems to take from me: he lets me feed with his hinds, bars me the place of a brother, and as much as in him lies, mines my gentility with my education
summary: 'Countenance' here means favor, recognition, or support — not merely a face. 'Hinds' are farm servants or laborers. 'Mines my gentility' uses 'mine' as a verb meaning to undermine or hollow out from below, as a mine digs beneath a wall to bring it down. Orlando is saying Oliver destroys his status as a gentleman (his 'gentility') by refusing him a gentleman's education, just as you would undermine a building's foundations.
detail: The phrase is a precise legal and social complaint. Gentility — gentry rank — was held to depend both on blood and on the behaviors (speech, manners, learning, horsemanship, swordsmanship) associated with that rank. By denying Orlando education, Oliver erodes the social expression of the birthright he cannot technically strip away. 'The something that nature gave me' (inborn rank, character, the father's spirit) is being hollowed out by Oliver's refusal to foster it.

anchor_text: The courtesy of nations allows you my better in that you are the first-born; but the same tradition takes not away my blood
summary: 'The courtesy of nations' means the convention agreed upon by civilized societies — in this case, the rule of primogeniture that gives everything to the eldest son. Orlando accepts that law: he acknowledges Oliver is his 'better' in rank and authority because he was born first. But he insists that no convention can strip him of his blood — his identity as their father's son and a gentleman by birth — however many brothers stood between them.
detail: Orlando's language is precise. He separates what custom grants (Oliver's superior position) from what nature gives (shared blood and the father's spirit). The phrase 'the same tradition takes not away my blood' is a direct challenge to any attempt to treat him as less than a de Bois: you may control the estate by law, but you cannot revoke his lineage. This distinction between inherited position and inalienable birth underlies the play's whole opening conflict.

anchor_text: elder brother, you are too young in this
summary: When Oliver calls Orlando 'boy,' Orlando retorts 'elder brother, you are too young in this.' The paradox is deliberate: you call yourself the elder, yet you are behaving childishly — too inexperienced in decent conduct, too immature in your treatment of a brother. Orlando deflects the insult by turning 'young' against Oliver, implying that seniority in birth confers no seniority in wisdom or right behavior.
detail: The exchange is a mini-battle over who has the higher claim to authority. Oliver asserts rank ('boy'); Orlando counters with conduct ('too young in this'). The legal status of being the firstborn — the 'elder' — is pointedly contrasted with the moral immaturity of acting as Oliver is acting. The wit is sharp: the very word that should prove Oliver's superiority (elder) is turned to show his deficiency.

anchor_text: Wilt thou lay hands on me, villain? ... I am no villain: I am the youngest son of Sir Rowland de Bois
summary: Oliver calls Orlando 'villain' as a term of abuse. Orlando rejects the word literally, not just emotionally: in its older legal sense, a 'villain' (from the Latin villanus, a serf) was a man of the lowest social class, bound to the land, with no free status. By calling him 'villain,' Oliver is trying to deny Orlando his birth-rank as a gentleman. Orlando answers by asserting his father's name — his lineage is his proof that he is no serf, and the same word used of his father would be the greatest possible insult.
detail: By Shakespeare's time 'villain' had already shifted toward its modern sense of a wicked person, but the feudal sense (a serf, a person of low birth, a churl without free standing) was still fully active. The ambiguity matters here: Oliver insults Orlando's character, but Orlando hears a slur on his rank and birth. Orlando's response — 'I am no villain; I am the youngest son of Sir Rowland de Bois' — equates his identity with his lineage rather than his conduct.

anchor_text: give me the poor allottery my father left me by testament; with that I will go buy my fortunes
summary: 'Allottery' is a word Shakespeare coins from 'allot' — it means a portion or share formally allotted, here the share of the estate that his father's will assigned to Orlando. Orlando asks for nothing more than what was legally set aside for him. 'Buy my fortunes' means use that sum to make my own way in the world — enter service, seek patronage, or try his luck.
detail: The scene has established that the thousand crowns were bequeathed by will; Oliver's charge was to use them to 'breed' Orlando as a gentleman. Orlando is now demanding either the education that was supposed to substitute for the money, or the money itself, so he can seek his fortune independently. Both requests are legally grounded: the father's will is the authority he repeatedly invokes. 'Buy my fortunes' carries the Elizabethan sense that prospects and advancement could be won by investment, patronage, or military service.

anchor_text: live like the old Robin Hood of England: they say many young gentlemen flock to him every day, and fleet the time carelessly, as they did in the golden world
summary: Charles describes Duke Senior's exiled life in the Forest of Arden in two literary images at once. 'The old Robin Hood of England' invokes the legend of the outlaw living freely in the greenwood with his band of 'merry men,' outside corrupt authority. 'The golden world' is the classical myth of a first age when humans lived without law, labor, or war, the earth yielding all things freely. Together they make Arden sound like a paradise of voluntary outlawry and primal ease.
detail: Ovid's Metamorphoses opens with the four ages of humankind (gold, silver, bronze, iron); in the Golden Age the earth was unploughed yet plentiful, there were no courts or kings, and people lived in perpetual spring. The Robin Hood tradition, reaching Shakespeare through medieval ballads and A Gest of Robyn Hode (printed c. 1500), added an English folk-version of the same freedom: the greenwood as a space of fellowship and rough justice outside a tyrannical law. Charles's one sentence layers classical myth over native legend to establish Arden as the play's escapist counter-world. As You Like It will spend most of its time testing whether either image is true.

anchor_text: an envious emulator of every man's good parts, a secret and villainous contriver against me his natural brother
summary: Oliver is lying directly to Charles about Orlando's character. The striking irony is that every charge Oliver levels at Orlando — envy, secret plotting against a brother, villainy — is precisely what Oliver himself is doing and will continue to do. Shakespeare gives Oliver a speech that is an unwitting self-portrait. 'Natural brother' means both a biological brother (born of the same father) and, ironically, the kind of brother that nature intends — a contrast to the unnatural behavior Oliver is enacting.
detail: This is the rhetorical figure of irony reinforced by dramatic irony: the audience, having just watched the scene between Orlando and Oliver, knows Oliver's slander is false. The word 'emulator' meant one who envies and tries to surpass another's achievements, with a strong sense of malice; 'contriver' meant one who plots by underhand means. Both terms fit Oliver exactly. The trick of projecting one's own faults onto the innocent party is the standard move of the play's stage villain, here set up in Oliver's first extended speech away from the honest confrontation with his brother.

anchor_text: he's gentle; never schooled and yet learned; full of noble device; of all sorts enchantingly beloved
summary: Alone after Charles leaves, Oliver suddenly confesses the truth his lies concealed: Orlando is everything he claimed he was not. 'Gentle' means both well-born and gracious in manner. 'Never schooled and yet learned' is the paradox of natural virtue — Orlando has the instincts and inner quality of an educated gentleman without formal education. 'Of all sorts enchantingly beloved' means every rank and class of person is drawn to him. Oliver's grudging inventory makes the audience understand why he hates his brother: not for Orlando's faults, but for his virtues.
detail: The soliloquy is a remarkable device: having just told Charles a string of falsehoods, Oliver turns and honestly enumerates Orlando's genuine qualities — then names pure envy as his motive ('for my soul, yet I know not why, hates nothing more than he'). The phrase 'I know not why' is important: Oliver cannot even justify his hatred rationally. 'Misprised' means wrongly assessed, undervalued, or despised — Oliver says he himself is 'altogether misprised' (overlooked and undervalued) next to Orlando's universal popularity, which is the true source of his resentment.

anchor_text: mock the good housewife Fortune from her wheel
summary: Fortune was imagined as a goddess who spins a great wheel, raising and casting down kings and commoners at random, blind to merit. Celia proposes that she and Rosalind 'mock' her off it — an irreverent fantasy that Fortune could be replaced by something fairer. The exchange that follows distinguishes Fortune (the world's random gifts of wealth and rank) from Nature (the gifts of beauty and wit).
detail: Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy (II, prose 1-2) gives the fullest medieval account of Fortune's wheel, and the image was so pervasive by 1600 that it needed no gloss — schoolchildren met it everywhere. The Fortune/Nature distinction Rosalind and Celia develop (TLN 171-72) is philosophically exact: Nature governs innate constitution (beauty, intelligence), while Fortune governs external circumstance (wealth, rank, power). The debate also frames the play's own action: the exiles in Arden must build a good life from Nature's gifts after Fortune has stripped them of rank.

anchor_text: the bountiful blind woman doth most mistake in her gifts to women
summary: Fortune was traditionally depicted as blind — she distributes her gifts without seeing who deserves them. Rosalind sharpens the complaint: Fortune most often gets it wrong specifically with women, giving beauty to the dishonest and virtue to the plain. Celia's punchline (TLN 168-70) supplies the logic: good looks attract corruption while plainness preserves innocence.
detail: The pun on 'honest' is important: 'honest' for a woman primarily meant 'chaste,' not merely truthful. So Rosalind's and Celia's riff implies that Fortune makes beautiful women unchaste (or at risk of being so) and virtuous women ugly — a standard Elizabethan satirical commonplace. The wit of the passage is that Rosalind and Celia are, by all evidence, both beautiful and virtuous, which is precisely what Fortune has failed to reward.

anchor_text: Fortune makes Nature's natural the cutter-off of Nature's wit
summary: A 'natural' was the Elizabethan word for a person with an intellectual disability — someone born, by nature, without full wit. Rosalind argues that it is Fortune's cruelty (not Nature's intention) that makes this particular 'natural' (Touchstone, a licensed court fool) the one to cut short their debate. There is also a teasing compliment: Touchstone may play the fool, but he interrupts the cleverest women in the court.
detail: The word 'natural' was not a polite term in Shakespeare's day, but its application to a court fool is complex: professional fools were called 'naturals' both because they were thought to have a native licence to speak truth and because the court kept both genuine simpletons and professional wits in the role. Touchstone is clearly the latter — a sharp professional — which is why Celia immediately turns the word around: his 'natural' wit, she implies, sharpens theirs like a whetstone (TLN 181-82), the punning name for a fool's function at court.

anchor_text: swore by his honour they were good pancakes
summary: Touchstone's joke turns on the logic of empty oaths: a man who swears 'by his honour' that a thing is so cannot be 'forsworn' (oath-breaking) if he never had any honour to swear by. The knight's oath was hollow from the start, so it cost him nothing to break it. The routine is a miniature sophism — a deliberate piece of false reasoning that happens to produce a technically correct conclusion, and it is Touchstone's first demonstration that a fool can tie reason in knots.
detail: The joke also works as a sly satire on Elizabethan dueling culture, in which noblemen swore constantly 'on my honour' to validate trivial claims. If the swearer lacked honour — through cowardice, debt, or disgrace — the oath was void before it left his mouth. Touchstone's point is that most courtly oaths are in this category. The same logic about degrees of oath and 'lying' will surface in the full 'degrees of the lie' treatise Touchstone delivers in Act 5.

anchor_text: whipp'd for taxation one of these days
summary: 'Taxation' here means censure or satirical criticism, not the levying of money. A court fool who mocked a nobleman too pointedly risked a real whipping — the lash was one of the standard punishments that reminded the fool his licence had limits. Celia is warning Touchstone to be careful about naming specific courtiers.
detail: The vulnerability of the licensed fool is a recurrent theme in Shakespeare: fools could speak truth only within limits, and when they overstepped, the 'allowed fool' became a plain fool who could be punished. In King Lear the Fool's disappearance after Act 3 may reflect the same dynamic — his speeches grow politically too dangerous to sustain.

anchor_text: fools may not speak wisely what wise men do foolishly
summary: Touchstone inverts the expected relationship between fools and wisdom: he complains that fools are not allowed to say wise things about the foolish things that wise men actually do. The antithesis ('fools... wisely'/'wise men... foolishly') is a chiasmus, and it is the play's clearest statement of the court fool's social function as truth-teller.
detail: This chiastic epigram encapsulates a tradition of praise of folly reaching back through Erasmus's Moriae Encomium (1511) to classical literature: the wise fool who sees clearly because he has nothing to lose. Celia immediately confirms it (TLN 208-10): since the little wit the fools are permitted has been 'silenced' by court censorship, the foolishness of the so-called wise men now fills the visible stage. Shakespeare returns to the same paradox in Lear's fool and Feste in Twelfth Night.

anchor_text: The Duke is humorous
summary: 'Humorous' in Shakespeare does not mean funny — it means governed by a particular mood or 'humour,' subject to sudden, unpredictable shifts of temper. A 'humorous' person had an imbalanced mix, making them capricious and volatile. Le Beau's quiet warning signals the turn the play is about to take: Frederick's 'humour' will soon produce Rosalind's banishment.

summary: 'Working-day' means ordinary, everyday, workaday — the world of duty and toil as opposed to 'holiday' or festival time. Rosalind is saying that the real world is full of thorns and difficulties, not the carefree space of the wrestling holiday just passed.

anchor_text: wrestle with thy affections
summary: Celia tells Rosalind to 'wrestle with' (fight, control) her feelings; Rosalind replies that her feelings 'take the part of a better wrestler' than she is. The sustained wrestling metaphor gives the conversation a wit that plays off the actual wrestling match in the scene just before, where Orlando threw Charles.

'Take the part of' means 'side with' or 'champion.' 'In despite of a fall' (TLN 401-402) means 'even after being thrown' — Celia predicts Rosalind will succeed in overcoming her feelings despite setbacks. The phrase 'hold intelligence with' was standard idiom for 'to be in regular contact or correspondence with.' Rosalind's argument runs: if she knows her own mind (she holds intelligence with herself), she can vouch that no treasonous thought has ever crossed it. The rhetorical form — 'if... if... if... then' — is formal and legalistic, showing Rosalind defending herself with the tools of rational argument against a charge that is purely irrational.

anchor_text: If their purgation did consist in words

detail: In early modern law and medicine 'purgation' had two related senses: the legal clearing of oneself from a charge through oath or evidence, and the medical purging of a humour or poison from the body. Frederick uses the legal sense: a formal acquittal or self-clearing by oath. The argument is circular and tyrannical — it admits no evidence in Rosalind's favour, since any protestation of innocence could equally be made by a guilty party. anchor_text: like Juno's swans, Still we went coupled and inseparable
summary: Celia compares herself and Rosalind to Juno's swans — the sacred birds of the queen of the gods — always paired and inseparable. The textual detail has puzzled editors since Theobald (1733), who proposed emending 'Juno' to 'Venus'; modern editors including Dusinberre (Arden 3, 2006) and Knowles (Oxford, 1977) retain 'Juno' as the Folio reading but note the confusion. One scholarly reading is that the Folio 'Juno' is simply a slip — by Celia, or by the compositor — and that 'Venus' would be metrically identical. Another is that the pairing of Juno (patroness of marriage) with the swans anticipates the play's wedding-drive. Either way, a student encountering the line would naturally ask which goddess owns the swans.

By Shakespeare's time the modern sense of inevitable, fatal destruction was developing, but the legal sense remained standard for formal judicial verdicts (OED s.v. anchor_text: with a kind of umber smirch my face
summary: 'Umber' is a brown pigment made from a natural earth mineral; 'smirch' means to daub or stain. Celia plans to darken her complexion with the pigment to look like a poor, sun-weathered countrywoman and so pass unrecognized on the road.
detail: Umber (raw or burnt) is still a standard artists' pigment, ranging from yellow-brown to dark brown. In the Elizabethan beauty standard a fair, light complexion was the mark of upper-class indoor life; a browned face signalled outdoor labour and low social rank. Darkening the face with umber was a conventional stage and narrative device for disguising a gentlewoman as a peasant or traveller. 'Smirch' (OED s.v. 'smirch' vb.) means to smear or soil — a light daubing, not a full theatrical blackface. The plan directly motivates why Celia will take the name 'Aliena' (the estranged outsider) and play a shepherdess in Arden, while Rosalind — taller and therefore better suited to pass as a man — takes the further step of full male disguise.

anchor_text: suit me all points like a man
summary: 'Suit me all points' means to dress myself in every detail as a man. Rosalind proposes to complete her male disguise with a 'curtle-axe' (a short cutlass or broad-bladed sword) on her thigh and a boar-spear in her hand — the weapons that would mark a young man of status.

The word derives from the Old French 'coutel' (knife) via 'courtelas'; Onions (Shakespeare Glossary s.v. 'curtle-axe') notes it as a variant of 'cutlass.' Rosalind's list — curtle-axe, boar-spear, gallant (brave/fashionable) bearing — are the props of a dashing young gentleman-hunter, precisely the persona she will sustain as 'Ganymede' in Arden. The boar-spear is a hunting weapon with a cross-piece below the head to stop the wounded animal running up the shaft — manly and dangerous in a way that suits her bolder plan.

anchor_text: Jove's own page, And, therefore, look you call me Ganymede
summary: Rosalind chooses 'Ganymede' as her male disguise-name. In myth, Ganymede was a beautiful Trojan youth carried off by Jove (Jupiter) to serve as cupbearer — 'page' — to the gods on Olympus. The name signals a lovely boy in powerful company, a plausible cover for Rosalind's tall, striking figure.

On the Elizabethan stage every female role was played by a boy, so 'Ganymede' creates an extra layer: a boy actor plays Rosalind, who disguises as a boy named for the most famous beautiful boy in classical myth. The name was also used as a common noun in English for a youth kept as a male lover; Marlowe's Dido, Queen of Carthage opens with Jupiter 'dandling Ganymede upon his knee,' so the erotic charge of the name would not have been lost on Shakespeare's audience. This disguise-name governs Rosalind's identity in Arden through Acts 2-5.

anchor_text: reference to my state: No longer Celia, but Aliena
summary: Celia's disguise-name 'Aliena' is Latin for 'the estranged one' or 'the alien' — someone cut off from their homeland and family. She is choosing a name that directly expresses what has happened to her: she has made herself a voluntary exile, alienated from her father's court.

By contrast Rosalind chooses a mythological alias (Ganymede) that says nothing about her inner state; Celia takes a name that is openly self-descriptive, pointing at the estrangement from her father she has chosen for love of her cousin. The name will resurface when Oliver, falling in love with her in Arden, knows her only as 'Aliena' — a stranger — which makes their love one of the play's purest, uncontaminated by prior knowledge of rank or history.

anchor_text: the penalty of Adam, -- The seasons' difference
summary: Duke Senior alludes to the curse God pronounces on Adam after the Fall: expelled from Eden, Adam must toil in a world of painful seasons and hard labor (Genesis 3:17-19). The Duke's point is wry -- he says the forest's biting cold is not the penalty of Adam but actually welcome, because unlike a flattering court it tells him the truth about his condition.
detail: In Genesis 3:17-19 (Geneva Bible 1599) God tells Adam: 'cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life.' The 'penalty' includes harsh weather and bodily suffering as marks of fallen humanity. Duke Senior's reversal -- finding moral benefit in what theology defined as punishment -- is characteristic of the play's pastoral argument: the forest's hardships are an honest education, superior to the comfortable deceptions of court. The golden-age fantasy (the classical equivalent of Eden before the Fall) is simultaneously invoked and qualified: this is no timeless paradise of eternal spring, but a real winter wood.

anchor_text: like the toad, ugly and venomous, Wears yet a precious jewel in his head
summary: Duke Senior draws on the widespread Elizabethan belief that the toad -- thought to be poisonous -- carried a gemstone called a 'toadstone' in its head, which had protective and medicinal powers. The paradox (something loathsome concealing something precious) is his image for adversity: painful on the outside, valuable within.
detail: The toadstone (lapis bufonis) was a standard entry in Renaissance natural-history and jewellery writing; Edward Topsell's Historie of Serpents (1608) discusses the belief, and it appears in Elizabethan amulet-lore as a remedy against poison. The folk-belief was that the stone changed colour on contact with venom, making it a living detector. Whether Shakespeare believed in it literally is beside the point: the image was culturally legible to any playgoer, and the paradox of beauty inside ugliness and profit inside pain is the speech's controlling figure. The rhetorical pattern -- apparent negative (ugly, venomous) then revealed positive (precious jewel) -- mirrors the larger argument: exile appears a harm, but yields self-knowledge.

anchor_text: poor dappled fools, Being native burghers of this desert city
summary: Two archaic words compress Duke Senior's unease about hunting. 'Burghers' (from Dutch burger) means citizens or freeholders -- the deer are the rightful inhabitants of this forest, not outsiders. 'Desert' here means deserted or uninhabited (a wilderness), not a sandy waste. Together the phrase casts the deer as lawful townspeople of a wild place the exiles have moved into uninvited.
detail: The irony is deliberate: the Duke uses the civic vocabulary of property and rights (burgher, native, confines, assign'd dwelling-place) to describe animals he is about to kill, then notes that Jaques accuses the hunters of being worse usurpers than Duke Frederick. 'Desert' in the sense of 'deserted, uninhabited' is recorded in Onions s.v. and in Schmidt s.v. as the primary Shakespearean sense here; it is unrelated to the modern geographical meaning. The Duke's word-choice signals a pastoral ethic that the play does not fully resolve -- the exiles claim to live simply and freely, but they still survive by killing the deer whose 'assign'd and native dwelling-place' they occupy.

anchor_text: The melancholy Jaques grieves at that; And, in that kind, swears you do more usurp Than doth your brother
summary: This is the play's first mention of Jaques, and 'melancholy' is his defining label from the start. 'Melancholy' in Elizabethan usage was not just sadness but a recognized temperamental type: a person dominated by black bile (one of the four bodily humours), prone to brooding, sharp social criticism, and fashionable gloom. Jaques immediately turns the hunters' pastime into a moral indictment -- the exiles are 'usurpers' of the deer's habitat, worse than the political usurper who banished them.
detail: The theory of the four humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) derived from Hippocrates and Galen and was standard Elizabethan medicine and psychology. Surplus black bile produced the melancholic temperament: withdrawn, satirical, and sharp-tongued. By 1600 the 'melancholy malcontent' had become a recognizable stage and social type -- the disillusioned traveller who cultivates sadness as a badge of superior sensibility. Jaques is Shakespeare's gentlest version of this type, more amused than bitter. His charge of 'usurpation' is a characteristic malcontent gesture: applying a political crime-word (usurp) to a recreational activity to expose an ethical contradiction the comfortable ignore.

anchor_text: thou mak'st a testament As worldlings do, giving thy sum of more To that which had too much
summary: Jaques compares the wounded deer weeping into the stream to a rich man leaving his money to someone already wealthy -- 'giving thy sum of more to that which had too much.' 'Worldlings' means people absorbed in worldly wealth. The image echoes the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:29): 'For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance.' Jaques turns it into a bitter commentary on how the fortunate get more and the wretched are abandoned.
detail: Matthew 25:29 (Geneva Bible 1599): 'For unto every one that hath, shall be given, and he shall have abundance.' The parable is about stewardship of gifts, but the surface logic -- abundance flows to abundance -- was proverbially cited as a statement about worldly injustice as much as divine economy. Jaques uses it satirically: the deer's tears, poured into an already full stream, are as pointless as leaving wealth to the already rich. A 'testament' is a last will and bequest; the deer on the verge of death is making a dying gift. The passage introduces Jaques's characteristic mode: taking a natural scene and distilling from it a maxim about human society.

anchor_text: Left and abandoned of his velvet friends; ''Tis right'; quoth he; 'thus misery doth part The flux of company'
summary: Jaques calls the deer's companions 'velvet friends' -- a biting double pun. Deer have a velvet-soft coat, but 'velvet' also signals expensive, soft courtly fabric and the smooth manners of those who flatter the powerful and desert them in misfortune. 'The flux of company' means the unstable, flowing crowd of fair-weather companions. The dying deer, deserted by the herd, becomes a figure for any disgraced person abandoned by those who once attended him.
detail: The pun works on two registers simultaneously. The literal: deer coats are soft, almost velvet-textured, especially in summer. The satirical: 'velvet' was expensive, courtly dress-material, and 'velvet friends' collapses the deer-companions into the time-serving courtiers who surround a powerful man, with their soft manners and promptly defecting loyalties. 'Flux' means flow, stream, and unstable movement -- the herd that flows past the dying deer mirrors the crowd that flows past a fallen favourite. Jaques's habit throughout the play is to read the natural world as a picture of human social behaviour, usually to the latter's discredit. This is his first extended example.

The irony is that Touchstone -- dismissed as mangy rabble by Frederick's court -- is the most linguistically accomplished figure who accompanies Rosalind into Arden.

anchor_text: The bonny prizer of the humorous duke
summary: 'Humorous' here means governed by a bad or unstable humour — an uncontrollable fit of ill temper or caprice. Elizabethans believed health and character were ruled by four bodily fluids ('humours'); a person dominated by any one of them to excess was described as 'humorous,' i.e., moody and unpredictable. Adam is saying Duke Frederick acts from irrational passion, not reason. 'Prizer' means a wrestler who wins a prize.
detail: The four humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) were thought to determine temperament; a man whose humours were out of balance was 'humorous' in the sense of erratic, subject to sudden moods. By the 1590s the word had acquired a theatrical currency — Ben Jonson's comedy of 'humours' made the concept a satirical fashion — but here Adam uses it clinically to diagnose Frederick's tyranny as a disorder of character rather than a deliberate evil. 'Bonny prizer' (a fine, prize-winning wrestler) has the colloquial admiring tone that makes Adam's warning vivid: Orlando's very excellence earned him the dangerous notice of an unstable ruler.

'Humorous' as capricious/ill-tempered from disordered humours is correct; the Jonson contextual aside is lightly proleptic (his Humour plays are contemporary with AYLI, not clearly prior) but is framed only as 'theatrical currency,' not claimed as a source, so it does not distort the gloss.

anchor_text: your virtues, gentle master, Are sanctified and holy traitors to you
summary: Adam uses an arresting paradox: Orlando's virtues are 'holy traitors' — things that are both sacred and treacherous at once. The phrase captures the play's central irony that goodness provokes envy and destruction in a corrupt court. 'Sanctified' means consecrated, blessed — yet those same blessings 'envenomin' and betray their owner.
detail: The rhetorical figure is oxymoron, combining contradictory terms (holy + traitor). Adam has already used a related paradox at TLN 626-627: 'what is comely / Envenoms him that bears it.' The sequence builds a small homily on the nature of virtue in a world governed by envy, a theme central to the play's movement from the corrupt court to Arden. The Biblical resonance of 'sanctified' is deliberate: it sounds like the language of sacred things, making the betrayal seem more outrageous.

anchor_text: malice Of a diverted blood and bloody brother
summary: 'Diverted blood' means blood (kinship, brotherhood) that has been turned away from its natural course. Oliver, who should love Orlando as a brother, has had his natural affection 'diverted' — redirected into hatred. 'Blood' meant both family relationship and one's shared nature as kin. Diverted blood is blood that has been dammed or turned back, so that natural warmth becomes unnatural enmity. The word 'bloody,' following immediately, plays on the same root with a different sense — violent. The near-pun on 'blood' in its two senses is typical of the play's language of nature subverted. Orlando's willingness to stay and die rather than steal is the moral contrast with Oliver that the scene is designed to establish.

anchor_text: He that doth the ravens feed, Yea, providently caters for the sparrow
summary: Adam invokes God's providence over even the least creatures: the God who feeds the ravens (Psalm 147 and Luke 12) and 'providently caters for the sparrow' (Matthew 10:29). Together they build the argument from lesser to greater: if God feeds animals, he will surely care for a faithful old man. The project has an existing card for the sparrow passage (Matthew 10:29) used in Hamlet; Adam's passage joins the raven to it. 'Providently' (adverb here, meaning 'with divine forethought') is itself a theological word.

anchor_text: in my youth I never did apply Hot and rebellious liquors in my blood
summary: 'Rebellious liquors' are hot, fiery drinks (wine and strong ale) that were thought to stir up the blood and inflame the 'rebellious' lower passions — lust, rage, excess. Adam boasts that his temperate youth explains his vigorous old age: he never fed his blood with stimulants that would throw his humours into disorder. 'Apply' here means to administer (a remedy or substance) to the body.
detail: Elizabethan medicine held that strong drink heated the blood and stimulated the appetite and passions — making it 'rebellious' because it incited the body to rebel against reason. The idea runs back through Galenic humoral theory: each of the four humours had associated qualities of heat and moisture, and excessive wine was thought to overheat the blood, promoting lust and aggression. Adam's restraint (he also avoided 'the means of weakness and debility,' i.e., sexual excess) follows the classical Stoic and Christian ideal of temperance as the foundation of long life. The speech echoes medical commonplaces familiar from John Cogan's Haven of Health (1584) and similar popular health guides, which Elizabethan readers would recognize.

anchor_text: constant service of the antique world, When service sweat for duty, not for meed
summary: Orlando praises Adam as a relic of an older, purer world where servants served out of loyalty ('duty'), not for wages ('meed'). 'Antique world' means the ancient past — here idealized as a golden age of faithful service, in contrast with the modern court where men work only to advance themselves. 'Meed' is an archaic word for reward or payment.
detail: The speech directly invokes the pastoral and golden-age idealization that structures the play. Orlando contrasts Adam's selfless fidelity with the self-interested service of the present age ('none will sweat but for promotion'), which echoes the classical topos of a lost golden world of natural goodness now replaced by an iron age of greed. Adam, carrying his life savings to give away, immediately becomes the living embodiment of the 'antique world' Orlando has just described — a point that gains ironic resonance when Jaques's 'seven ages of man' speech (2.7), delivered just after Adam is carried in half-dead, closes with 'sans everything.' The 'antique world' is here both a moral standard and a theatrical warm-up for the golden-world debate that runs through Arden.

anchor_text: thou prun'st a rotten tree, That cannot so much as a blossom yield In lieu of all thy pains and husbandry
summary: Orlando compares himself to a dead tree that Adam is trying to cultivate, extending the metaphor across three lines: pruning a tree that cannot blossom, meaning all of Adam's care and effort ('pains and husbandry') will go unrewarded. 'Husbandry' here means careful, thrifty tending — the same word used for farming. The metaphor of the fruitless tree was a familiar scriptural and proverbial image for wasted effort.

'Prun'st' contracts 'prunest' (early modern spelling); 'in lieu of' means 'in return for.' The image of the unfruitful or dead tree had a wide biblical resonance (Matthew 3:10, 'Every tree which bringeth not foorth good fruite, is hewen downe and cast into the fire'), but Orlando uses it without scriptural heat — it is a practical gardening metaphor, which gives the moment warmth rather than theology.

anchor_text: O Jupiter! how weary
summary: Rosalind swears by Jupiter, the king of the Roman gods, rather than by God or Christ. Characters in As You Like It use pagan oath-words throughout ('Jove,' 'Jupiter,' 'Hercules') — a conventional dramatic distancing that placed the play in a pre-Christian pastoral world and kept it clear of blasphemy laws.
detail: The Elizabethan Act to Restrain Abuses of Players (1606) forbade using the name of God, Jesus Christ, or the Holy Ghost on stage, which pushed writers toward classical substitutes. In As You Like It the pattern is consistent: Rosalind also swears 'by my life' and 'Jove! Jove!' (TLN 740), and Orlando invokes 'Jove' and 'Hercules.' The pagan oath-words suit the pastoral-classical world the play inhabits and signal a literary register distinct from the London present.

anchor_text: comfort the weaker vessel, as doublet and hose
summary: Rosalind says she must 'comfort the weaker vessel' — a phrase from 1 Peter 3:7, where husbands are told to give honour 'unto the wife as unto the weaker vessel.' She casts herself in the husband's role because she is wearing male dress ('doublet and hose'), while the exhausted Celia ('Aliena') plays the part of a woman in need of comfort. The joke turns on her cross-dressing.
detail: The Geneva Bible's 1 Peter 3:7 ('Likewise ye husbands, dwell with them as men of knowledge, giuing honour vnto the woman, as vnto the weaker vessell') was a standard text on the duties of marriage. By citing it, Rosalind frames her disguise humorously: 'doublet and hose' (men's jacket and fitted leg-coverings) and 'petticoat' (the skirt marking a woman) stand in for the husband-and-wife roles of the epistle. The comedy of the scene depends on the audience knowing that the 'man' speaking is a woman played by a boy actor.

anchor_text: bear no cross if I did bear you; for I think you have no money
summary: Touchstone packs three meanings into 'cross': (1) to bear a burden or trouble, (2) to carry a cross (as in suffering), and (3) a cross as a coin — old English coins often bore a cross on the reverse side. He says he would 'bear no cross' (suffer no hardship, and have no money) if he carried Celia, since she appears to have no coins left. The joke signals the trio's poverty and Touchstone's wordplay habit.
detail: The monetary sense of 'cross' was well established: the standard English penny bore a cross on its reverse, so 'not a cross' meant penniless. Touchstone layers the theological bearing of a cross onto the financial and physical senses, compressing all three into one clause. This kind of multiple-pun wit is his characteristic mode. Onions (Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'cross') records the coin sense as current and notes its use in several Shakespearean puns.

anchor_text: actions most ridiculous Hast thou been drawn to by thy fantasy
summary: 'Fantasy' here does not mean imagination or daydream in the modern sense; it means passionate, irrational love — the inner compulsion that drives a lover to absurd behavior. Silvius is asking Corin how many foolish acts love's obsession has made him commit.

summary: 'Wearing' here means wearing out, exhausting, or wearying — not wearing as in clothing. anchor_text: the wooing of a peascod instead of her; from whom I took two cods
summary: A 'peascod' is a pea-pod; Touchstone, so deluded with love for Jane Smile, wooed a pea-pod as if it were the girl herself. A 'cod' is the pod or husk that encloses seeds; he took two pods and gave them back to Jane as love-tokens with weeping 'Wear these for my sake.' The joke presents his young love as ludicrously rustic and abject.
detail: The passage is also lightly bawdy at the scholar level: 'cod' was common Elizabethan slang for a scrotum (compare 'cod-piece,' the padded front-flap of men's breeches). Touchstone 'took two cods' from the peascod and presented them to the girl — an innuendo about giving a woman what is meant for a man. The bawdy is secondary and the passage works at face value as a parody of pastoral love-token exchange, but a London audience attuned to Touchstone's style would catch the double sense. See Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'cod' (sense 2).

anchor_text: all is mortal in nature, so is all nature in love mortal in folly
summary: Touchstone's sentence reverses its own terms: 'all is mortal in nature' becomes 'all nature in love [is] mortal in folly.' The figure is antimetabole — repeating words in reverse order to sharpen a point — and the effect is that love's folly is as universal and inescapable as death. Rosalind rightly notes he speaks 'wiser than thou art ware of': the fool has stumbled into a truth.
detail: Antimetabole (reversing key words from one clause to the next: A-B / B-A) was a formal rhetorical scheme taught in Elizabethan grammar schools from Quintilian and Erasmus. Here the chiastic flip ('mortal in nature' / 'nature in love mortal') converts a general observation about death into a comic assertion that love turns all of nature into a fool. 'Mortal' shifts sense between the two halves: in the first it means 'subject to death'; in the second it intensifies to 'extreme, absolute' (as in 'mortal enemy'). The Arden editors note this as one of Touchstone's characteristic moves: an accidental philosophy stumbled on through wordplay. See Onions, s.v. 'mortal' (sense 2: used as an intensive).

sources.name: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria
sources.citation: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 9.3.85 (antimetabole as a figure of repetition by inversion); cf. Erasmus, De Copia (1512), on the school-taught figures of repetition. Onions, C. T. Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'mortal' (sense 2: as an intensive, 'extreme, exceeding').

Identifying the figure as antimetabole is correct — the A-B/B-A inversion is textually plain — and the observation that 'mortal' shifts from 'subject to death' to an intensive ('extreme') between the two clauses is a defensible and useful reading, not an overreach.

anchor_text: I am shepherd to another man, And do not shear the fleeces that I graze
summary: Corin is not a landowner but a hired shepherd: he tends someone else's flock and cannot offer hospitality because the sheep's wool ('the fleeces') belongs to his master, not to him. This detail distinguishes him from the idealized literary shepherd of pastoral romance; he is a wage laborer without property, and his honest acknowledgment of it marks him as the play's 'real' countryman against the courtly pretense of pastoral.
detail: In Elizabethan sheep-farming, a hired shepherd received wages and sometimes a small percentage of the flock, but the wool and the pasture were the landowner's. That Corin cannot 'shear the fleeces he grazes' is a precise economic statement: he lacks the autonomy to trade or give food, and his master is absent and 'churlish' (gruff, ungenerous). This is the scene that introduces the play's court-versus-country debate — Corin's honest poverty contrasted with both courtly superficiality and literary pastoral fantasy. His voice here anticipates his debate with Touchstone in 3.2.

Corin's status as a hired (not freehold) shepherd is precisely what the text states, and the distinction between the idealized literary shepherd and an economic wage-laborer is a mainstream critical point grounded in the play's court-versus-country debate; the reading does not overreach.

anchor_text: little recks to find the way to heaven By doing deeds of hospitality
summary: 'Little recks' means cares little. Corin says his master is stingy with hospitality and does not use it as a means of earning salvation ('finding the way to heaven'). In Elizabethan England, open hospitality to travellers and the poor was widely understood as a Christian duty and a mark of the gentry's social obligations — refusing it was a sign of moral failure.
detail: The Elizabethan ideal of 'good housekeeping' (lavish hospitality from the great house to neighbors, travelers, and the poor) was both a social norm and a theological claim: almsgiving and hospitality were works of mercy that pointed toward salvation. Ballads, homilies, and complaint literature of the period lamented the 'decay of hospitality' as wealthy landowners enclosed land and retreated to London. Corin's remark thus casts his absent master in the contemporary role of the 'uncharitable' new landlord who has abandoned rural duties — a socially pointed observation dressed in pastoral terms.

anchor_text: Under the greenwood tree, Who loves to lie with me
summary: Amiens sings the play's first forest song, celebrating Arden as a place without enemies except 'winter and rough weather.' The 'greenwood' is the traditional English folk-name for a forest where outlaws and free men live beyond the reach of court and law — the world of Robin Hood — and Duke Senior's exiled company has been likened to that tradition in Act 1. The song enacts rather than argues the play's pastoral ideal.
detail: The greenwood of English ballad tradition is a space outside normal hierarchy where fellowship replaces rank; Duke Senior's band in Arden has already been called 'like the old Robin Hood of England' (1.1). Amiens's song is a recruitment lyric: it promises that whoever 'loves to lie' (to rest) under the trees and match his voice to the birds will find no enemy except the weather. The refrain's promise of no enemy but winter quietly tests the golden-world fantasy the play has been building — Arden is benign but not perfect, and the 'icy fang' of winter is real. In As You Like It songs carry the pastoral argument without stating it: this one does the work of Duke Senior's 'sweet are the uses of adversity' speech (2.1) in lyric form.

anchor_text: I can suck melancholy out of a song, as a weasel sucks eggs
summary: Jaques describes his ability to drain a song of all its sadness the way a weasel drains an egg — sucking out the nourishing part and leaving the empty shell. The boast defines his character: where others hear cheer in the forest songs, Jaques extracts gloom, because he cultivates melancholy as a deliberate pose. In Elizabethan medical theory, melancholy was caused by excess black bile and was considered both a disease and a mark of deep intelligence.
detail: The four Elizabethan humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) were thought to govern temperament; too much black bile produced the melancholic — brooding, detached, sardonic. By 1600 the stage malcontent had made melancholy fashionable: the travelling, disillusioned wit who stands apart from life and rails at its folly. Jaques is the play's benign version of this type, and his line here is almost a self-advertisement. The weasel simile is precise and slightly comic: weasels do pierce eggshells and drain the contents whole, and the image reduces Jaques's grand grief to a small animal's trick. Amiens's mild warning ('It will make you melancholy, Monsieur Jaques') only prompts the delighted 'I thank it' — Jaques wants to be sad.

anchor_text: that they call compliment is like the encounter of two dog-apes
summary: 'Compliment' here means the formal exchange of thanks and courtesies — what we might call polite small talk or social ritual. Jaques dismisses it as no better than two dog-apes (male baboons) sniffing and grimacing at each other: the bodily ritual of the animal world dressed up as manners. The joke is that thanking someone 'heartily' feels to Jaques like the greeter is offering a beggarly coin and expecting gratitude in return.

anchor_text: He is too disputable for my company
summary: 'Disputable' means 'argumentative' or 'inclined to dispute' — Duke Senior engages too readily in philosophical debate and Jaques, who hoards his own gloom privately, finds this irritating. Jaques says he thinks just as much, but keeps it to himself and gives heaven thanks. The irony is that Jaques is himself the play's most relentless arguer; what he dislikes in the Duke is the cheerful, grateful version of his own brooding.

anchor_text: Ducdame, ducdame, ducdame
summary: When Amiens asks what 'ducdame' means, Jaques answers deadpan: ''Tis a Greek invocation, to call fools into a circle.' The word is Shakespeare's own coinage — it appears nowhere else — and Jaques is joking. The 'Greek invocation' is a mock-learned explanation for a nonsense refrain, and the 'fools' called into the circle are the lords who have abandoned wealth and ease to follow a banished duke into the forest, including Jaques himself.
detail: Editors have proposed many derivations — the Welsh 'dewch da mi' ('come to me'), a corrupt Latin phrase, a garbled Italian command — but none is convincing, and the joke works best as deliberate nonsense, a parody of the meaningless refrains common in popular song. Jaques has written his own satirical verse to the tune Amiens sang, replacing the golden-world invitation ('who loves to live i' the sun') with a caustic one ('if any man turn ass, leaving his wealth and ease'), and his refrain is a wordless, fake-solemn 'come hither' for fools. The wit doubles back: everyone listening, including Jaques, has done exactly what the song mocks.

anchor_text: rail against all the first-born of Egypt
summary: If Jaques cannot sleep, he says he will 'rail against all the first-born of Egypt' — meaning he will curse everything indiscriminately, as dramatically as possible. The 'first-born of Egypt' refers to the tenth and worst of God's plagues on Pharaoh: God killed the first-born child in every Egyptian household in one night to compel Pharaoh to release the enslaved Israelites. To 'rail against' such victims is to rage against the most grievously afflicted — Jaques threatens to howl at maximum volume at maximum misfortune.
detail: The plague of the first-born is recounted in Exodus 12:29-30 (Geneva 1599). The phrase is Jaques's comic hyperbole for a sleepless night of railing: just as he will suck melancholy out of any available source, he will direct his grumbling at the most pitiable target imaginable, an entire nation's bereaved parents. The allusion is knowingly excessive — it implies no actual sympathy for Egypt — and is typical of Jaques's sardonic self-dramatization.

anchor_text: uncouth forest yield anything savage
summary: 'Uncouth' here means unknown, strange, or wild — not rude or socially awkward as it does today. Orlando is calling the forest an unfamiliar, uncharted wilderness, not a discourteous one.
detail: The older sense of 'uncouth' (Old English uncuth, 'unknown') survived in literary and poetic contexts through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. It commonly described wild, trackless, or unfrequented places. The word's modern meaning (coarse in manners) is a later narrowing. Spenser uses the word in the same topographical sense in The Shepheardes Calender; Milton uses it similarly in Comus (1634). The OED cites this line under 'uncouth' sense 2, 'strange, unusual, unfamiliar' (OED s.v. 'uncouth,' adj., sense 2).

anchor_text: Thy conceit is nearer death than thy powers
summary: 'Conceit' means imagination or mental conviction, not vanity or a clever metaphor as it usually means today. Orlando is telling Adam that his mind has given up sooner than his body has actually failed: 'you think you are dying, but your body is stronger than you believe.'
detail: In Elizabethan English 'conceit' (from Latin concipere, 'to conceive') covered any mental conception, idea, or imagined notion — including the self-persuading belief that one is near death. The line is a practical pep-talk: the collapse is psychological before it is physical, and the mind can be rallied even when the body is weak. The medical idea that a patient's mental state hastened or delayed death was a commonplace of Galenic humoral medicine. Compare Othello 3.3.151 ('a conceit more rich in matter') and Sonnet 15 ('conceit deceitful') for the same broad semantic range.

anchor_text: For my sake be comfortable
summary: 'Be comfortable' is not a request to relax. In Elizabethan English 'comfortable' meant 'capable of giving comfort' or 'able to take comfort.' Orlando is urging Adam to cheer up and summon his spirits — 'comfort yourself' — not to make himself physically at ease.
detail: The word derives from Latin confortare ('to strengthen greatly'). In Shakespeare's usage, 'comfortable' and its cognates most often carry the active sense of giving or receiving strength and consolation rather than physical ease. The modern sense of physical convenience or well-being is largely a later development. Compare Richard III 1.3, where Queen Elizabeth calls Buckingham 'my comfort' (a strengthening presence), and Measure for Measure 3.1, where the Duke asks Isabel to 'be comfortable to my mother.' The adverb 'comfortably' in the sense 'with cheer and courage' is cited in OED from texts throughout this period.

anchor_text: anything in this desert
summary: 'Desert' here means an uninhabited, deserted wilderness — not a sandy, arid landscape. Orlando is calling the Forest of Arden a wild, unpeopled place, emphasizing how isolated and alone they are, with no settlement nearby to beg food from.
detail: The word comes from Latin desertum, 'a place forsaken or abandoned,' from deserere, 'to desert, abandon.' In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries 'desert' (or 'desart') routinely meant any uninhabited tract — forest, moor, or mountain — regardless of climate or terrain. The OED gives Shakespeare's own forests as examples of the sense. The same usage appears at 2 Henry VI 3.2 ('And more than so, in low-bent fawning' — where 'desert' is a place without people) and, closer to hand, in As You Like It itself: Duke Senior earlier speaks of finding 'tongues in trees, books in the running brooks' in this same 'desert city' (2.1) — a self-consciously paradoxical phrase for a forest of solitude. The sense clarifies Orlando's meaning: if there is any living thing — animal or plant — in this wilderness, he will bring food.

anchor_text: compact of jars, grow musical, We shall have shortly discord in the spheres
summary: Duke Senior jokes that if Jaques — 'compact of jars' (made up of quarrels and discords) — has turned musical, then even the heavens must be going wrong. The 'spheres' refers to the ancient idea that the planets were set in concentric crystal spheres whose perfect, silent rotation produced a divine 'music of the spheres.' Discord there would mean cosmic disorder.
detail: Ptolemaic cosmology placed the earth at the centre of a series of nested transparent spheres carrying the moon, sun, and planets; their harmonious revolution was thought to produce an inaudible celestial music (musica mundana). The joke inverts this: Jaques, whose natural element is discord (jars = discords, disagreements), turning musical signals that the normally harmonious spheres must have gone dissonant. The image belongs to a tradition running from Plato's Republic (10.617) through Cicero's 'Dream of Scipio' and Boethius; Shakespeare returns to it in The Merchant of Venice 5.1 ('There's not the smallest orb which thou behold'st / But in his motion like an angel sings').

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary

The inversion joke — Jaques (made of discord) turning musical implies the harmonious spheres have gone wrong — is a sound, mainstream reading of a clear ironic quip, and the Ptolemaic / musica mundana background is well-supported.

anchor_text: A motley fool;--a miserable world!
summary: 'Motley' was the parti-coloured coat — patched in two or more colours — that was the official dress of a licensed court jester. Wearing it marked a man as the fool whose job was to speak home truths without being punished. Jaques is thrilled because a 'motley fool' (Touchstone) has been philosophizing about time: the fool's coat is the one garment that gives its wearer absolute licence to criticize.
detail: A licensed fool (Latin: stultus) was kept by aristocratic and royal households to entertain and deflate pomposity; his motley gave him legal and social immunity — what he said in 'his motley' could not be taken seriously or punished as slander. The excitement Jaques feels is that the costume he craves is the only one that licenses open social satire. 'A miserable world' is the fool's punchline: time passes and we are no wiser. The phrase 'Motley's the only wear' (TLN 887) caps the speech as a wish to don that immunity.

anchor_text: he drew a dial from his poke, And, looking on it with lack-lustre eye, Says very wisely, 'It is ten o'clock
summary: A 'dial' is a sundial or pocket watch (early portable sundials were the era's timepieces). A 'poke' is a bag or pocket. Touchstone pulls out his watch-dial and stares at it with bleary, 'lack-lustre' (dull, lifeless) eyes, then delivers his mock-profound meditation on the passing of time.

anchor_text: from hour to hour, we ripe and ripe, And then, from hour to hour, we rot and rot
summary: The lines work on two levels at once: the 'hour to hour' rhythm mimics the clock's ticking, and 'ripe / rot' is both literal (fruit ripening and rotting) and a bawdy pun. 'Hour' was pronounced like 'whore' in Elizabethan English, so 'from whore to whore, we ripe and ripe' — we grow by sleeping around and then decay from it — is the joke Jaques hears and laughs so hard at. The pun encodes the fool's whole moral: time passes, pleasure rots.
detail: The 'hour' / 'whore' pun was standard Elizabethan wordplay; 'ripe' could mean sexually mature (compare 'ripe' in Hamlet 3.4), and the biological arc from youth to decay was a commonplace memento mori. That the fool delivers this bawdy philosophy so solemnly — with 'lack-lustre eye' — is what strikes Jaques as both funny and true. The 'thereby hangs a tale' capping it off (TLN 881) is another bawdy pointer: 'tale' / 'tail' (backside) was a standard pun.

anchor_text: My lungs began to crow like chanticleer
summary: Chanticleer is the name of the rooster in the medieval beast-fable tradition, most familiar from Chaucer's 'Nun's Priest's Tale' in The Canterbury Tales. To say that Jaques's lungs 'crowed like Chanticleer' means he laughed so hard that his laughter sounded like a cock crowing — a comparison that also gently mocks the self-important crowing of any learned commentator.

anchor_text: O that I were a fool! I am ambitious for a motley coat
summary: Jaques's 'ambition for a motley coat' is a deliberate paradox: ambition (the desire to rise) usually aims at power, wealth, or glory — not a jester's patched uniform. He wants the fool's coat precisely because it lowers its wearer's social status to zero, and in doing so grants total freedom of speech. The wit of the line is that the highest freedom (to speak truth to power) requires wearing the lowest costume.

summary: A 'charter' is a written grant of rights and privileges, such as a royal charter that permits a town to hold its own court or market. Jaques wants a charter — a formal grant of licence — as unlimited as the wind, which blows on anyone without asking permission. The metaphor is apt: the wind cannot be sued for libel, and neither should the licensed fool.

anchor_text: they that are most galled with my folly, They most must laugh
summary: 'Galled' means chafed, stung, or wounded — the image is of a horse rubbed raw by an ill-fitting saddle. Jaques's logic is that the person most hurt ('galled') by the fool's satire is forced to laugh it off: if he shows he is wounded, he reveals that the cap fits him. 'The bob' (TLN 909) means a taunt or blow. 'Anatomiz'd' (TLN 910) means dissected, exposed — the wise man's hidden folly is cut open and displayed by the fool's casual hit.

summary: A 'counter' was a blank metal disc used in arithmetic and as imitation coin — worthless as real currency but useful for keeping score. Jaques insists he would not harm anyone 'for a counter,' i.e. for something of no real value; he is worth nothing to the vices he attacks because he attacks them in general, not by naming specific people. The phrasing also implies he would not accept even a token payment to do harm.

anchor_text: thou thyself hast been a libertine, As sensual as the brutish sting itself; And all the embossed sores and headed evils
summary: Duke Senior punctures Jaques's satirical pose: you have been a 'libertine' — a man of unrestrained, dissolute life — and your proposed satire would only discharge your own vices onto the world. 'Embossed sores' means swollen, festering boils (embossed = swollen, puffed out like a boss on a shield); 'headed evils' are abscesses with a gathered head. The Duke accuses Jaques of suffering from symptoms of syphilis, a venereal disease acquired by his own 'sensual' licence.

'Brutish sting' refers to animal lust; 'embossed sores' and 'headed evils' are medical terms — swollen pustules (embossed from the Latin bossa, a rounded protuberance) that critics from the 17th century onward have taken as signs of the 'French disease' (syphilis). That Jaques would 'disgorge' these diseased contents into the world makes his satire a form of infection.

anchor_text: the thorny point Of bare distress hath ta'en from me the show Of smooth civility: yet am I inland bred
summary: Orlando apologizes for bursting in with a drawn sword: sheer hunger ('bare distress') stripped him of 'smooth civility' (polite manners). anchor_text: All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players
summary: Jaques's 'Seven Ages of Man' speech weaves together two ancient ideas: the theatrum mundi ('world as a stage'), a commonplace from classical antiquity, and the division of a human life into seven ages, linked to the seven planets. He counts them: infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, pantaloon (old man), and finally 'mere oblivion.' The speech is a brilliant set-piece, but the play frames it as Jaques's characteristic melancholy: he turns a life into a pageant of decay.

summary: A 'pard' is a leopard (from Latin pardus). The soldier age is defined by a spotted beard, touchiness about honor ('jealous in honour' = hypersensitively defensive of his reputation), and readiness to fight over any slight. 'Bubble reputation' captures how quickly military fame pops: a man will risk death at the cannon's mouth ('even in the cannon's mouth') for a 'bubble' — something hollow and quick to burst.

anchor_text: the justice, In fair round belly with good capon lin'd, With eyes severe and beard of formal cut, Full of wise saws and modern instances
summary: The 'justice' (a magistrate or justice of the peace, one of the most important figures of local Elizabethan government) is satirized as fat, pompous, and well-bribed. A 'capon' was a fattened castrated rooster, a gift routinely given to judges and magistrates to secure favorable rulings — so 'capon lin'd' means literally stuffed with bribery. 'Wise saws' are proverbs or maxims; 'modern instances' are up-to-date illustrations or precedents — the justice's speeches are full of clichés.

anchor_text: The sixth age shifts Into the lean and slipper'd pantaloon, With spectacles on nose and pouch on side; His youthful hose, well sav'd, a world too wide For his shrunk shank
summary: The 'pantaloon' was a stock character from Italian commedia dell'arte — a lean, doddering, miserly old man, usually named Pantalone, who wore slippers and spectacles and was the butt of every joke. He kept his old youthful breeches ('hose') but they now hang baggy on his shrunken legs ('shrunk shank'). Jaques imports this stock comic figure to characterize the age of decline — a theatrical type for a theatrical speech.
detail: Commedia dell'arte, the popular Italian improvised-comedy tradition, had fixed character types in masks: the Pantalone (miser, merchant, foolish old man) was one of the most recognizable. By Shakespeare's day English audiences would have known the type from touring Italian companies and from its echoes in English drama. 'Slipper'd' marks him as indoors, past active life; the too-wide hose (knickerbockers) measure the physical collapse of the body. 'Shank' = lower leg, tibia. The detail is precise: a prosperous man's expensive clothes, carefully saved for decades, now fit nothing.

sources.name: Lea, Italian Popular Comedy
sources.citation: Lea, K. M. Italian Popular Comedy: A Study in the Commedia dell'Arte, 1560-1620. 2 vols. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1934, vol. 1, pp. 44-52 (Pantalone, the Venetian merchant type).

The commedia dell'arte Pantalone as stock miserly old man in slippers and spectacles is the correct identification; the detail about expensive hose saved for decades now hanging on shrunken legs is an accurate, non-speculative reading.

anchor_text: Is second childishness and mere oblivion; Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything
summary: Jaques ends the Seven Ages with a figure called anaphora — the same word ('sans') repeated at the head of each clause for emphasis. The four-fold 'sans' strips away the senses one by one, and 'sans everything' leaves nothing. 'Second childishness' means a return to helplessness and dependence, completing the cycle: the speech opened with a mewling infant and closes with someone equally unable to function. 'Mere oblivion' means absolute, total forgetting — the self dissolves.

sources.name: Lanham, Handlist of Rhetorical Terms
sources.citation: Lanham, Richard A. A Handlist of Rhetorical Terms. 2nd ed. U of California P, 1991, s.v. 'anaphora' (the repetition of the same word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1021

Identifying the four-fold 'sans' as anaphora is correct; 'second childishness' as return to helplessness completing the infant-to-oblivion cycle is the mainstream reading; 'mere oblivion' as total dissolution is accurate.

anchor_text: Blow, blow, thou winter wind, Thou art not so unkind As man's ingratitude
summary: Amiens's song compares the hurt of cold weather unfavorably to the hurt of human ingratitude and forgotten friendship: the wind at least is not being 'unkind' on purpose, because it has no mind to intend cruelty. The song voices the play's central court-versus-country theme: the physical hardships of the forest are honest and clean; the 'unkindness' of false friends at court is worse because it is deliberate. 'Heigh-ho' is a sigh or melancholy cry; the holly was an evergreen symbol of endurance through winter.
detail: The song is built on a series of contrasts — winter wind / man's ingratitude; bitter sky / benefits forgot; the sting of weather / the sting of a friend forgotten. The refrain ('Most friendship is feigning, most loving mere folly') is close to cynical, yet the chorus insists 'This life is most jolly' — the paradox that a harder but honest life in the forest beats the duplicity of court. The evergreen holly framing the refrain reinforces the theme of something constant surviving winter. Duke Senior has made a version of this argument more prosaically at 2.1 ('sweet are the uses of adversity').

The court-versus-country reading of the song — natural hardship is honest, courtly ingratitude is worse because deliberate — is the standard, well-grounded interpretation supported by Duke Senior's 2.1 speech; the holly-as-endurance emblem is defensible.

anchor_text: Though thou the waters warp
summary: 'Warp' here means to freeze, cause to contract and distort — as frost warps standing water into ice or makes pools ripple and buckle with cold. The song uses the image to measure natural violence (frost warping water) against something worse: a friend who, now that fortune has changed, forgets the kindnesses done for him ('benefits forgot').

Glossing 'warp' as frost causing water to freeze and distort is the accepted sense in this context; the use of the image to contrast natural violence with the sharper sting of forgotten friendship is a sound, textually supported reading.

anchor_text: If that you were the good Sir Rowland's son,-- As you have whisper'd faithfully you were, And as mine eye doth his effigies witness Most truly limn'd and living in your face
summary: Duke Senior recognizes Orlando partly by what Orlando has told him and partly by his face, which carries his father's likeness. 'Effigies' means image or likeness (from Latin effigies, a portrait or representation). 'Limn'd' means painted or drawn — the face is described as a living portrait that 'paints' Sir Rowland's image with perfect fidelity. The recognition scene links Orlando to the Duke's world and explains the warmth of the welcome.

anchor_text: were I not the better part made mercy
summary: Duke Frederick means: 'if I were not more than half composed of mercy' — that is, if mercy were not the larger share of his nature. 'The better part' = the greater portion; 'made' = constituted, made up of. The phrase 'seek an absent argument of my revenge' follows: argument here means 'subject' or 'occasion,' so he would not go hunting for a subject (Orlando, who is absent) for his vengeance when the very person he wants to punish (Oliver) stands before him. The logic is a threat: Oliver is already within reach of the Duke's anger.
detail: The compressed syntax bundles two ideas: Frederick claiming a merciful nature while simultaneously threatening maximum violence. 'Argument' in the sense of 'subject of an action or proceeding' is common in Shakespeare (cf. Hamlet 1.1: 'We do it wrong... to let the warrant of our argument expand'); here it ironically measures the Duke's mercy — he won't punish the absent Orlando through the present Oliver, but only out of supposed clemency, not principle. The speech establishes Duke Frederick as the play's tyrant: fluent, self-justifying, and dangerous.

anchor_text: Seek him with candle
summary: The phrase echoes the parable of the lost coin in Luke 15:8, where a woman lights a candle and sweeps the whole house to find a coin she has lost. Frederick is telling Oliver to search with the same obsessive thoroughness — leave no corner unexamined. For Shakespeare's audience, primed on the Geneva Bible read aloud weekly in church, the reference would be immediate.

The woman's candle-and-sweeping search (15:8) is the middle one. Here Duke Frederick inverts the parable's tenderness -- the woman rejoices to find the lost coin; Frederick wants Orlando found 'dead or living.' The biblical echo gives his command a sardonic undertone: he will seek this 'lost' young man with the same thoroughness as a woman seeking her coin, but without any of the rejoicing.

anchor_text: quit thee by thy brother's mouth
summary: 'Quit' here means 'acquit' — to clear someone of a charge or accusation. 'Quit thee by thy brother's mouth' means: get yourself cleared of suspicion by having Orlando himself testify for you (or confess his own guilt). Oliver's lands are seized 'till' he can produce Orlando, whose own statement will either exonerate Oliver or confirm the charges against him.
detail: The legal sense of 'quit' (= acquit, discharge from an obligation or accusation) is the primary meaning throughout the period. Compare 'quitclaim' in property law, where one party renounces a claim on another. The phrase makes explicit that Oliver is being held as a quasi-hostage or a suspect in Orlando's disappearance: only Orlando's own voice ('mouth') can discharge him. The construction is archaic but precise — it foreshadows the plot dynamic in which Oliver must seek the brother he despises in order to recover what he has lost.

anchor_text: Make an extent upon his house and lands
summary: A 'writ of extent' was an Elizabethan legal instrument that allowed the Crown (or a creditor) to seize and value a debtor's property — lands, goods, and chattels — as security for a debt or penalty owed to the sovereign. Duke Frederick is ordering his officers to execute exactly this kind of royal confiscation on Oliver's estate. The phrase would have been recognizable legal vocabulary to Shakespeare's audience.
detail: The writ of 'extent' (from the Latin extendere, to value and survey) originated in medieval common law as the Crown's remedy against debtors. Under it, a royal officer called the escheator would enter the debtor's lands, survey them ('extend' = assess the value), and take possession on the sovereign's behalf. In practice it was also the instrument by which an attainted or politically disfavored subject could be swiftly dispossessed without a formal conviction — making it here a tool of tyranny barely dressed in legal form. The scene mirrors the play's larger theme: the usurping Duke Frederick exercises the same arbitrary power over Oliver that he has exercised over Duke Senior and over Rosalind. The word 'expediently' (TLN 1075) — meaning 'speedily' (not 'conveniently') — enforces the urgency: the confiscation is to happen at once, before Oliver can resist.

sources.name: Blackstone, Commentaries
sources.citation: William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England (1765-69), Vol. III, ch. 26, on writs of extent and the Crown's right to extent lands for debt; the instrument was active throughout the Elizabethan period.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'extent' n., sense 5: 'A writ directing the sheriff to cause lands of a debtor to be appraised at their full (extended) value.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1074

Blackstone, Commentaries Vol. III ch. 26 ('Of Execution') genuinely discusses the writ of extent/extendi facias as the Crown's mechanism to appraise and seize a debtor's lands, and the OED sense cited for 'extent' as a writ directing the sheriff to appraise lands at full extended value is accurate.

A 'writ of extent' as a Crown instrument for seizing and valuing a subject's property is accurate common-law history, the Elizabethan sense of 'expediently' as 'speedily' is correct, and the thematic parallel to Frederick's earlier dispossessions is textually grounded rather than speculative.

anchor_text: thrice-crowned queen of night, survey
summary: Orlando addresses the moon-goddess in her triple form: Cynthia (moon in the sky), Diana (huntress on earth), and Hecate (goddess of darkness below). 'Thrice-crowned' refers to the crescent, full, and new phases of the moon, or to these three divine identities. 'Thy huntress' name' points to Rosalind, whose name contains Rosa ('rose') but whose association here is with Diana's chaste, silver light.
detail: The triple moon-goddess was a Renaissance commonplace, synthesized from Hesiod (Theogony 411-452) and Ovid (Metamorphoses 7.94-99). By invoking her Orlando casts Rosalind as a Petrarchan unattainable, a Diana-figure whose huntress power over him is absolute. The speech is deliberately overblown, setting up Touchstone's mockery that follows.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1077

The triple-goddess synthesis (Cynthia/Diana/Hecate) is a Renaissance commonplace well attested in Ovid and elsewhere, and the framing of Rosalind as a Petrarchan Diana-figure whose 'huntress name' governs Orlando is directly supported by lines 1077-1079; the note that the speech is 'deliberately overblown' anticipates Touchstone's parody and is a mainstream editorial reading.

'Character' as a verb meaning to engrave or inscribe is squarely supported by the line and by standard Elizabethan usage; the etymology from Greek kharakter is accurate and uncontroversial.

anchor_text: The fair, the chaste, and unexpressive she
summary: 'Unexpressive' here means inexpressible or impossible to fully describe in words — beyond expression. It does not mean 'expressionless.' The line closing Orlando's poem says Rosalind's qualities surpass what any language can capture.

anchor_text: how like you this shepherd's life, Master Touchstone
summary: This exchange launches the play's central court-vs-country debate. Touchstone's deliberately self-contradicting logic — the shepherd's life is both good and naught, both pleasing and tedious — parodies the formal rhetorical exercise of arguing both sides of a question (the disputatio). The word 'in respect of' means 'considered as' or 'from the perspective of.'

Touchstone is turning it into a comic routine. The debate between court refinement and country simplicity is the play's spine, drawn from Thomas Lodge's Rosalynde (1590) and ultimately from the classical pastoral tradition — Theocritus, Virgil's Eclogues — which imagined a simpler world as a mirror for courtly vice.

sources.name: Lodge, Rosalynde

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1086

Touchstone's self-contradicting 'in respect of' logic as a parody of argumentum in utramque partem is the standard mainstream reading; the debate's Lodge/pastoral ancestry is accurate and the annotation does not overreach.

anchor_text: Such a one is a natural philosopher
summary: Touchstone's pun runs two ways. 'Natural' means 'of or concerning nature' (Corin's earthy wisdom is a philosophy of natural life), but 'natural' also meant a born idiot or simpleton in Elizabethan English. So Touchstone calls Corin both a 'nature philosopher' and a 'natural fool' in the same breath.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1103
