The double sense of 'natural' — nature-philosopher and born idiot — is well established in Elizabethan usage and is the obvious pun in context; the annotation is accurate and measured.

anchor_text: thou art damned, like an ill-roasted egg
summary: Touchstone constructs a mock syllogism: no court = no good manners; no good manners = wickedness; wickedness = damnation. The absurd result is that Corin is damned simply for never having visited a city. The comparison to 'an ill-roasted egg, all on one side' means half-cooked — singed on one face, raw on the other — which mocks the logic as lopsided nonsense. The whole speech parodies the formal logical disputation of the schools.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1108

The annotation correctly identifies the mock syllogism (no court → no good manners → damnation) and the 'ill-roasted egg, all on one side' as mocking lopsided reasoning; both readings are standard and directly supported by the scene text.

anchor_text: perfumed with civet
summary: Civet is a strong, musky perfume extracted from the anal glands of the civet cat — a luxury scent fashionable at court. The joke deflates courtly refinement by revealing its animal origins.

anchor_text: sighing every minute and groaning every hour would detect the lazy foot of time
summary: Rosalind's wit-exchange with Orlando about clocks sets up her famous speech on time's different paces. Orlando says there is no clock in the forest; Rosalind counters that a true lover's sighs and groans mark time more reliably than a clock face. The pun is on the clock's 'foot' (one tick, from the pendulum's 'foot') and time's 'lazy' movement when nothing is happening.

anchor_text: Time travels in divers paces with divers persons
summary: Rosalind's extended conceit classifies four types of people and the pace at which time seems to move for each — ambles, trots, gallops, or stands still. The rhetorical form is division (divisio), a schoolroom exercise of exhaustively parcelling a topic into its sub-types. The four categories are: young bride-to-be (trots = slow); comfortable priest and comfortable rich man (ambles = easy); thief going to execution (gallops = too fast); lawyer on vacation (stands still). The speech shows off Rosalind's verbal wit as much as it teaches anything about time.

anchor_text: quite traverse, athwart the heart of his lover; as a puny tilter
summary: Celia uses the image of an incompetent jouster to mock Orlando's oath-breaking. In a tilt (a mounted lance-combat), the rider must aim his lance straight at the target; a bad ('puny') tilter runs 'traverse' -- crosswise, at an angle -- and his lance breaks 'athwart' (sideways across) the target rather than hitting it clean. Orlando's vows strike Rosalind's heart at the same useless angle.

'Traverse' means running across the line of the course rather than along it -- the beginner's error that wastes the charge and breaks the lance sideways instead of point-on. 'Puny' (from French puine, 'born after') meant junior, inexperienced, raw -- a puny tilter is a novice whose horse he cannot control. 'A noble goose': goose here means fool or simpleton; the staff breaking slantwise makes him look magnificent in the wrong way. The jousting metaphor is fitting: Orlando won Rosalind's attention by throwing the professional wrestler Charles (1.2), an act of genuine strength; now Celia demotes him to a bungling horseman.

anchor_text: common executioner, Whose heart the accustom'd sight of death makes hard
summary: Professional hangmen and headsmen at public executions in Elizabethan England were required by custom to ask the condemned person's forgiveness before carrying out the sentence — a ritual acknowledgment that the killer acted under the law's order, not personal malice. It was a gesture meant to preserve the moral innocence of the state officer and the dignity of the condemned. Silvius's compressed simile uses it as a benchmark for basic human decency: if even a man hardened by daily death still observes this courtesy, Phebe's scorn is crueller than the scaffold.

anchor_text: eyes,--that are the frail'st and softest things, Who shut their coward gates on atomies,--
summary: 'Atomies' means tiny specks of dust — literally the smallest conceivable particles. Phebe's argument is logical: eyes are so delicate that they involuntarily close against the merest dust-mote, so they can hardly be weapons capable of murdering a man.

anchor_text: cicatrice and capable impressure Thy palm some moment keeps

'Cicatrice' (from Latin cicatrix) was a medical term for scar tissue; Shakespeare uses it elsewhere (e.g., All's Well 2.3 'my cicatrice looks raw and red'). 'Capable impressure' fuses 'capable' in the sense of 'receptive, able to hold' (OED adj. 4) with 'impressure' meaning a pressed-in mark (from Latin impressura). anchor_text: wounds invisible That love's keen arrows make
summary: Silvius invokes the standard classical image of Cupid, the Roman god of love, whose arrows strike the heart and cause the 'invisible wounds' of passion. He is telling Phebe that when she herself falls in love she will understand how love wounds without leaving a visible scar.

Here the allusion is doubled: Silvius uses the very cliche Phebe has been demolishing (that eyes are murderers), but relocates the wounding from her eyes to Love's arrows. anchor_text: no more in you than in the ordinary Of nature's sale-work

anchor_text: your inky brows, your black silk hair, Your bugle eyeballs
summary: 'Bugle' here means black and shiny, like a bugle-bead — a small, tubular, jet-black glass bead used in Elizabethan embroidery and ornamentation. anchor_text: down on your knees, And thank heaven, fasting, for a good man's love
summary: Rosalind tells Phebe she should kneel and give thanks for Silvius's love even on an empty stomach — 'fasting,' meaning without any feast or celebration — because she should count it a blessing, not take it for granted. The gesture of kneeling reinforces Rosalind's lesson that Phebe's proper attitude toward Silvius is humble thankfulness, not disdainful superiority.

anchor_text: Dead shepherd! now I find thy saw of might; 'Who ever loved that loved not at first sight?'
summary: Phebe quotes a line from Christopher Marlowe's poem Hero and Leander (1598) — 'Who ever loved that loved not at first sight?' — calling him 'Dead shepherd' because Marlowe was killed in 1593. anchor_text: I shall think it a most plenteous crop To glean the broken ears after the man That the main harvest reaps
summary: Silvius uses the image of gleaning — gathering the leftover grain ('broken ears,' i.e. stalks of wheat) that a harvester drops after the main crop is cut. The practice is drawn from the book of Ruth, where the poor were permitted by law to follow reapers and gather what was left. Silvius means he will be content with the scraps of Phebe's attention — an occasional smile — that fall from her preoccupation with 'Ganymede.'

The Mosaic law required landowners to leave the edges of the field and the fallen stalks for the poor (Leviticus 19:9-10). Shakespeare's Elizabethan audience would have recognized the allusion at once, since Ruth's devotion and poverty were widely cited as models of faithful loyalty. Silvius casts himself as the destitute gleaner — grateful for whatever negligible kindness falls from the main 'harvest' of Phebe's love for another.

anchor_text: omittance is no quittance

anchor_text: scholar's melancholy, which is emulation
summary: Jaques catalogues seven varieties of melancholy matched to seven social roles: the scholar's melancholy is caused by professional envy (emulation); the musician's by wild imagination (fantastical); the courtier's by pride; the soldier's by ambition; the lawyer's by scheming; the lady's by fastidiousness (nice); the lover's by all of these at once. His own he calls a unique compound extracted from wide travel and observation. The seven types mirror the 'seven ages of man' scheme Jaques delivered in 2.7.

Timothy Bright's A Treatise of Melancholie (1586) and later Robert Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy (1621) codified its varieties. Jaques's connoisseurship of melancholy types -- finding all of them insufficient for his own refined version -- is the self-parody of a man who prizes his own sadness as a personal distinction. The word 'simples' (TLN 1739) means the individual herbal ingredients compounded into a medicine, a figure from apothecary practice: Jaques's melancholy is a custom blend, not an off-the-shelf variety.

anchor_text: sold your own lands to see other men's
summary: Rosalind skewers the fashionable Elizabethan traveller who spent his inheritance touring the Continent to acquire foreign manners and came back with nothing but affectation. Rosalind's teasing at TLN 1753-1757 -- telling Jaques he must lisp, wear strange suits, and disparage his own country to prove he has swum in a gondola (the fashionable Venetian conveyance) -- belongs to this tradition of anti-travel satire.

anchor_text: he carries his house on his head; a better jointure
summary: Rosalind's snail joke works on two levels. On the surface: a snail arrives slowly but comes equipped with a house (his shell), which makes him a better marriage-provider ('jointure' = property settlement guaranteed to a wife) than Orlando. The second level: snails carry horns -- the Elizabethan emblem of the cuckold, the man whose wife has been unfaithful. Rosalind says the snail 'brings his destiny with him,' meaning the horns are already on him so he can never be newly cuckolded by a wife.
detail: The word 'jointure' (TLN 1772) is a legal term for the property settlement a husband guarantees to his future wife, paid on his death or the marriage's breakdown -- a tangible sign of commitment Orlando has not offered. The horn-joke riffs on the anxiety that any husband may be cuckolded and the snail's advantage is that he is already 'armed' with his horns, thus 'prevents the slander of his wife' (TLN 1776-1777): he cannot be further dishonoured. Rosalind, disguised as 'Ganymede' and directing her own mock-courtship, gets to voice male anxieties about marriage with impunity.

anchor_text: die by attorney. The poor world is almost six thousand years old
summary: When Orlando says he will 'die' if refused -- conventional Petrarchan hyperbole where to be denied is to die of love -- Rosalind demolishes the conceit with comic logic. anchor_text: Troilus had his brains dashed out with a Grecian club
summary: Troilus was the Trojan prince who loved the Greek girl Cressida; he became the type of the faithful, suffering romantic hero. Troilus was considered one of the great 'patterns of love,' which is exactly the romantic inflation Rosalind is puncturing.

In the Troy legend Troilus was killed by Achilles or by a Grecian weapon in battle, not by love-sickness. Rosalind's joke is to give this death the most banal, physical explanation possible -- a club -- against the lovers' tradition of poetic languishing.

anchor_text: Leander, he would have lived many a fair year, though Hero had turned nun
summary: Leander swam the narrow Hellespont strait each night to visit Hero, his beloved, guided by a lamp in her tower. One stormy night the lamp was blown out; he lost his way and drowned. Rosalind retells the story as pure bathos: Leander did not die for love but because he was a bad swimmer who got a cramp on a hot midsummer night, and the 'foolish chroniclers' who blamed Hero were wrong. The deflation of the most famous love-death in ancient literature drives home her point that 'men have died from time to time, and worms have eaten them, but not for love.'

By having Rosalind reduce the lovers to a boy with cramp and a lampless night, Shakespeare deflates Marlowe's lush epyllion with comic precision. The phrase 'Hero of Sestos' (TLN 1812) is an allusion to Hero's home town, Sestos on the European bank of the Hellespont -- a detail from Marlowe's own poem.

anchor_text: men are April when they woo, December when they wed
summary: Rosalind delivers a rapid-fire antithetical proverb: men are spring (eager, fresh, courtly) while wooing, and winter (cold, settled, indifferent) once married; women are May (in bloom) while still maids, but the sky changes once they are wives. She then launches into a comic catalogue of impossible wifely behaviour she promises to inflict on Orlando -- weeping like Diana in the fountain, laughing like a hyena at wrong moments -- to brace him against the reality of marriage.

The 'Barbary cock-pigeon' (TLN 1850) is a pigeon from the Barbary coast (North Africa), famous for jealous possessiveness over its mate -- a jest about how jealous Rosalind intends to be. The hyena (TLN 1854, spelled 'hyen') was popularly thought to laugh, a classical and bestiary commonplace ultimately rooted in Pliny's account of the beast in Natural History Book 8.

The three-stage escalation (a rhetorical tricolon) makes the point through comic accumulation. 'Casement' is a hinged window that opens outward, like a modern French window.

anchor_text: your doublet and hose plucked over your head, and show the world what the bird hath done to her own nest
summary: Celia reproves Rosalind for 'misusing' womanhood in her love-talk while disguised as a man. A doublet and hose was the standard Elizabethan male outfit: a close-fitting padded jacket (doublet) and tight-fitting breeches (hose). Celia threatens to strip these off over Rosalind's head, exposing that she is a woman dressed as a man, and 'show the world what the bird hath done to her own nest' -- meaning the bird (Rosalind) has fouled her own nest (dishonoured her sex) with her frank love-talk.

Celia applies it to Rosalind's performance as 'Ganymede': by speaking so boldly about the mechanics of love and the failings of wives, Rosalind has misrepresented -- or over-represented -- what women are and think. The threat of public unmasking ('show the world') also underscores the theatrical risk of the whole disguise plot.

anchor_text: that same wicked bastard of Venus, that was begot of thought, conceived of spleen, and born of madness
summary: Rosalind describes Cupid, the god of love, as a 'wicked bastard of Venus' -- calling him illegitimate because in some classical traditions his father was uncertain. He was 'begot of thought' (born from the mind's fantasy), 'conceived of spleen' (the spleen being the Elizabethan seat of sudden impulse and passion), and 'born of madness.' He is blind ('his own are out'), which is why he makes fools of everyone else's eyes by shooting them with love against their better judgment.
detail: In classical mythology Cupid's parentage was debated: most commonly he was the son of Venus (Aphrodite) and Mars, but other versions made him self-generated or the child of various gods. The 'bastard' tag here probably draws on the tradition Ovid uses in Metamorphoses 1 and elsewhere, where Cupid is presented as wayward, ungovernable, and capricious -- a child who toys with the gods themselves. The 'spleen' was in Elizabethan physiology the organ of sudden impulse, caprice, and passionate laughter or spite. That Cupid is blind and punishes others' eyes while his own are sightless is the standard Ovidian conceit: he causes the irrational, unseeing condition of love in others.

anchor_text: present him to the duke, like a Roman conqueror
summary: A Roman general who won a major victory was awarded a 'triumph' — a formal parade through Rome with his army, spoils, and captives. Jaques adapts the ceremony for a hunt: the man who killed the deer will be presented to Duke Senior with the animal's horns on his head, as a captured enemy's spoils might crown a triumphant soldier.
detail: The Roman triumph was voted by the Senate only for a victory over a foreign enemy; Julius Caesar was criticised for celebrating a triumph over fellow Romans after Munda (45 BCE). Shakespeare's company would have staged Roman triumphs in Julius Caesar and Coriolanus, making the image immediately recognisable. Jaques's mock-heroic application — dressing a deer-hunter as a conquering general — is deliberately absurd, and sets up the horn-joke that follows: the 'branch of victory' he proposes is antlers, not laurel, so the 'triumph' is really a cuckold-crowning.

The mock-triumph reading is fully grounded in the text ('present him to the duke, like a Roman conqueror') and the antlers-as-spoils extension is a natural, mainstream inference from the scene's logic.

anchor_text: deer's horns upon his head for a branch of victory
summary: Victorious Roman generals were crowned with a wreath of laurel, and any outstanding deed of arms earned a special 'crown' of leaves or grass — a 'branch of victory.' Here Jaques proposes the deer's antlers as a substitute garland, turning the hunt into a mock-triumph and setting up the horn-song's joke about cuckolds.
detail: Several Roman honor-crowns existed: the corona civica (oak leaves for saving a citizen's life), the corona graminea (grass for rescuing an army), and the laurel wreath of the triumph. All were 'branches' of honor in the general sense Shakespeare uses. The joke depends on the double meaning of 'horn': the deer's antler (a hunting trophy) and the horn traditionally said to grow on the forehead of a man whose wife is unfaithful. Jaques is already preparing the comic ground for the song that follows.

Reading 'branch of victory' as a laurel-garland analogue is sound; the annotator correctly notes the double payoff (wreath → antlers → cuckold's horn) that sets up the song, and the OED sense for 'branch' as trophy or garland is a defensible support.

anchor_text: Take thou no scorn to wear the horn
summary: The entire horn-song works on a double meaning: the deer's antler as a hunting trophy, and the 'horn' supposedly worn on a cuckold's forehead — a man whose wife has been unfaithful. The song insists the hunter need not be ashamed of his horns because they are, in fact, every man's hereditary property: his father wore them, his grandfather before him, and so on back to Adam.
detail: The Elizabethan cuckold joke was that an unfaithful wife caused her husband to sprout invisible horns, visible to everyone except the wearer — his public mark of shame. Because horned deer were killed in the hunt, hunting itself became a running bawdy metaphor: to 'hunt' was to pursue sexual conquest, and the hunter's trophy was both animal antler and the cuckold's horn. The song makes the joke universal — no man can escape the horns because no man can be certain of his ancestry — which is the same logic Touchstone deploys elsewhere in the play. The song's refrain 'the lusty horn / Is not a thing to laugh to scorn' defuses male anxiety by making cuckoldry comic and inevitable. Jaques's enthusiasm for the song fits his pose as a detached, worldly observer who enjoys pricking human pretension.

anchor_text: It was a crest ere thou wast born
summary: A 'crest' is the decorative device on top of a heraldic coat of arms — the family badge worn on a helmet. The song claims the horn is the hunter's hereditary crest, meaning he was born into it; his family has 'worn the horn' for generations. The joke is that a crest is a mark of lineage and pride, while the cuckold's horn is a mark of shame — yet the song insists they are the same thing, and every family has one.
detail: In Elizabethan heraldry the crest sat atop the helm and identified the bearer's lineage; a man's crest was his to inherit. The horn-as-crest gag therefore runs: if cuckoldry is inherited, it is no disgrace — it is simply the family tradition. The following two lines ('Thy father's father wore it; / And thy father bore it') push the genealogy back two generations, and 'bore it' puns on 'bore' meaning both 'carried' and the past tense of 'bear' (to endure), suggesting the horn is something every man carries and every man must put up with. The whole sequence is a mock-blazon — a parody of heraldic praise.

anchor_text: man as rare as Phoenix
summary: The Phoenix was a mythical bird of which only one existed in all the world at any time; it lived for hundreds of years, then burst into flames and was reborn from its own ashes. The line doubles as ironic comedy: Phebe is telling the 'youth' she passionately desires that she does not desire him.

anchor_text: she defies me, Like Turk to Christian
summary: The Ottoman ('Turkish') empire and Christian Europe were in a state of near-constant warfare throughout the sixteenth century, and 'Turk' was an Elizabethan byword for an implacable, ruthless enemy. To defy someone 'like Turk to Christian' is to invoke the most absolute imaginable hostility — two sides with nothing in common and no possibility of mercy.
detail: The Ottoman advance into southeastern Europe, the fall of Constantinople (1453), the siege of Malta (1565), and the Battle of Lepanto (1571) kept the Turk-Christian conflict vividly present in English consciousness. On the Elizabethan stage 'Turk' and 'infidel' were interchangeable terms for a merciless, alien adversary; Elizabeth I made diplomatic overtures to the Ottoman Sultan Murad III, so the political picture was complicated, but 'like Turk to Christian' functioned as a fixed idiom for total enmity, as Rosalind uses it here.

anchor_text: Such Ethiop words, blacker in their effect
summary: 'Ethiop' is an Elizabethan spelling of 'Ethiopian,' meaning a dark-skinned African. Rosalind is extending her comparison of the letter to foreign aggression: the words are 'blacker in their effect / Than in their countenance' — they appear dark on the page (ink on paper) but their hostile meaning is even darker than their colour.
detail: The conceit works on two registers. First, it is a visual pun: written words are literally black (ink), and 'Ethiop' triggers the association with blackness. Second, Rosalind claims the effect of the words — the cruelty they enact on Silvius — exceeds even their black appearance, which is the deeper insult. The comparison follows a common Elizabethan rhetorical habit of linking darkness with moral hostility (compare 'blacker than a coal' in other contexts). Modern editors note the passage is not simply racist abuse but a rhetorical spiral from the 'Turk' comparison: foreign enemy, dark ink, hostile meaning, all stacked. Students should note that Elizabethan usage of such comparisons reflects the period's racial vocabulary, not any annotation endorsement of it.

anchor_text: Art thou god to shepherd turn'd
summary: Phebe's letter casts 'Ganymede' as a god who has disguised himself as a shepherd to walk among mortals — a recurring motif in classical myth, where gods take human or pastoral form to approach mortals they desire. The most pointed parallel is Apollo, who served as a shepherd for King Admetus as a divine punishment; but the question also glances at Jove's pursuit of Ganymede, whose name Rosalind is wearing as her disguise.

Phebe, an educated pastoral speaker (she quotes Marlowe at 3.5), consciously frames her infatuation in these terms, which lends a comic irony: she is addressing a woman disguised as a youth named for Jupiter's own boy-beloved, asking whether a god is hiding in shepherd's clothing. The question is truer than she knows.

anchor_text: scorn of your bright eyne
summary: 'Eyne' is a poetic plural of 'eye,' already archaic in Shakespeare's day but kept alive in verse for its elegiac and romantic sound. It appears here inside Phebe's letter, which is written in rhymed couplets — a signal that it is a love-poem as much as a letter, and Phebe is deploying the worn vocabulary of the lovelorn Petrarchan lover.

Its appearance in Phebe's letter is tonally significant: she claims to despise 'Ganymede' but is writing poetry to him, complete with antique poetic vocabulary. Compare Sidney, Astrophil and Stella, and Spenser's sonnets, which regularly use 'eyne.' Rosalind's sardonic interruptions mock the very genre Phebe is unwittingly performing.

anchor_text: Would they work in mild aspect
summary: 'Aspect' is an astrological term: the angular relationship between planets in a horoscope, which determines whether their combined influence is 'mild' (benign) or harsh. Phebe is imagining that 'Ganymede's' scornful glance has the power of a harsh planetary aspect — and asking what would happen if those eyes instead turned a 'mild aspect' upon her.
detail: In Elizabethan astrology the aspects were specific angles (conjunction, trine, sextile, square, opposition) between planets in the natal chart, each with a defined influence on human fortune and temperament. A 'mild aspect' would be a trine or sextile, considered beneficial. The transference of astrological language to a human gaze — treating the loved one's eyes as a planetary influence shaping the lover's fate — was a convention of Petrarchan love poetry, fully canonised in Sidney's Astrophil and Stella ('With how sad steps, O Moon, thou climb'st the skies'). Phebe's use of the term here signals her literacy in that convention; Shakespeare also uses 'aspect' in its astrological sense in Sonnet 26 and elsewhere.

anchor_text: in the purlieus of this forest
summary: 'Purlieus' (singular: 'purlieu') are the outlying parts of a forest — the fringe land where the forest blends into cultivated or open ground. Specifically in English law, a purlieu was land once included in a royal forest but later disafforested, which retained certain forest customs. Oliver is asking for the location of a sheep-cote that sits on the forest's edge.

The legal sense — land on the outer boundary of a forest — had been in common use since the thirteenth century and was familiar to Elizabethan audiences. Here it simply denotes the forest's margin, where a working sheep-farm (a 'sheep-cote') could plausibly be located.

anchor_text: Chewing the food of sweet and bitter fancy
summary: Oliver describes Orlando walking through the forest lost in lovesick thoughts — 'fancy' here means love or romantic longing. The phrase uses the image of a ruminating animal chewing its cud to capture the repetitive, slow turning-over of a lover's mixed feelings ('sweet and bitter' because love brings both joy and anguish). It is a compressed metaphor that tells us Orlando's mind was entirely on Rosalind as he walked.

'Fancy' in Elizabethan English routinely meant romantic love or infatuation (compare Olivia's 'Is't not well done?' / 'Excellently done — if God did all' in Twelfth Night 1.5, and the song 'Tell me where is Fancy bred' in The Merchant of Venice 3.2). The bittersweet quality — 'sweet and bitter' — echoes the Petrarchan oxymoron of love as both pleasure and pain.

anchor_text: green and gilded snake had wreath'd itself
summary: The scene of a sleeping man threatened by a snake coiling toward his mouth, then a lioness crouching nearby, is a deliberate piece of emblematic natural history — a double danger that requires a hero to rescue his sleeping enemy. Renaissance natural history (Pliny, Topsell) held that a snake entering a sleeping person's mouth was a recognized peril; the lioness's attribute (below) adds a second emblem. Together they stage Orlando's decision as a test of magnanimity.

The green-and-gilded snake recalls the traditional association of serpents with treachery and the garden of Eden; its 'indented glides' (looping, angular movements, like indentations on a serpent's belly) are observed detail. The pairing of serpent-threat and lion-threat — a sleeping man between two dangers — recalls emblem-book conventions in which the tested hero must choose nobility over revenge. The scene functions as Oliver's 'conversion narrative': he is saved by the brother he has wronged, and the rescue transforms him.

anchor_text: royal disposition of that beast To prey on nothing that doth seem as dead
summary: Oliver states it as a fact of natural history that a lion will not attack anything that appears to be dead — only living prey. This belief (that lions are too noble to strike what is motionless and seemingly lifeless) was a commonplace of Elizabethan natural history writing, representing the lion as a creature of royal magnanimity that disdains ignoble kills. Oliver's sleeping body therefore survives only because he looked dead.

The lion's 'royal disposition' was an accepted topos in Elizabethan England: the lion as king of beasts, with a magnanimity and selectiveness befitting royalty. The idea is part of the heraldic vocabulary of royalty (the lion rampant, the royal arms). Here it serves a narrative function: Oliver is saved by a natural law that mirrors the moral law Orlando must also overcome -- his own 'just occasion' for revenge.

anchor_text: kindness, nobler ever than revenge
summary: Oliver encapsulates Orlando's moral victory in a sententious couplet: both 'kindness' (benevolent feeling toward kin — 'kind' derives from 'kin,' the same nature) and 'nature' (natural love of family) overcame Orlando's 'just occasion' for revenge against the brother who had tried to kill him. The phrase 'nobler ever than revenge' is a deliberate moral maxim — a pithy general truth — of the kind that the genre of comedy uses to mark a character's conversion.
detail: The Elizabethan word 'kindness' carried a double weight now faded: it meant both benevolence and the natural bond of kinship ('kind' = kin, family). Orlando's act is thus simultaneously a generous choice and a natural one, which is exactly the paradox Oliver articulates: 'kindness... and nature' are grammatically parallel, two names for the same impulse. The sententia ('kindness, nobler ever than revenge') is characteristic of the play's moral register, where maxims punctuate the action. The same ethical claim underlies Prospero's famous 'The rarer action is / In virtue than in vengeance' (The Tempest 5.1).

anchor_text: sweet Ganymede
summary: Rosalind faints at the sight of Orlando's blood-stained handkerchief, involuntarily breaking her male disguise. When she recovers, she scrambles to explain it away: the swoon was 'counterfeited' — an act, a piece of performance. Oliver, watching, does not believe her. The scene turns on the collision between her real feelings and the role she has been playing, and it is the first time her composure as 'Ganymede' fully cracks.
detail: The moment is structurally and theatrically charged. Rosalind has maintained her Ganymede persona through the bawdy, teasing sessions of Act 3-4, but the sight of Orlando's literal blood dissolves it. Her attempt to reclaim the performance ('Counterfeit, I assure you') fails: Oliver's line 'there is too great testimony in your complexion' invokes the period's belief that involuntary physical signs (blushing, pallor, fainting) could not be faked and revealed inner truth. Oliver's final 'You lack a man's heart' is simultaneously a simple observation and a dramatic irony: she does lack a man's heart because she has a woman's one. On the Elizabethan stage a boy actor playing Rosalind playing Ganymede faints for love of a man — the multiple layers of performance and gender are never closer to the surface. Celia's slip ('Cousin') at TLN 2086 is a matching involuntary betrayal of the disguise.

anchor_text: a most vile Martext
summary: Sir Oliver Martext is a hedge-priest whose name is a joke: to 'mar a text' means to garble or bungle a passage of scripture. Touchstone called off the wedding in Act 3 because Jaques warned that a marriage performed by someone who 'mars texts' would be irregular and effectively void. The name mocks ignorant country clergy who could not read their own liturgy.
detail: An ordained Anglican priest was required to read the wedding service correctly from the Book of Common Prayer (1559); a 'martext' who garbled the words might cast doubt on the marriage's validity. Jaques's objection in 3.3 ('and not being well married, it will be a good excuse for her hereafter to leave her husband') turns on exactly this legal hazard: an irregular ceremony was grounds for the couple to part. The name belongs to a tradition of satirical naming for low clergy in Elizabethan comedy (compare Holofernes the pedant-parson in Love's Labour's Lost); here the joke is that Touchstone half-wanted the bad ceremony precisely for its built-in escape clause.

anchor_text: meat and drink to me to see a clown
summary: 'Meat and drink' means pleasure and sustenance — the two things a person most needs. Touchstone is saying that watching a simple rustic is his deepest enjoyment. 'Clown' here does not mean a circus comedian; it is Elizabethan for a country bumpkin or uneducated rustic, as opposed to the wit of a courtier or a professional fool.
detail: The phrase 'meat and drink' as an expression of something intensely satisfying is proverbial in Elizabethan English and persists in modern 'it is meat and drink to him.' 'Clown' in Shakespeare's usage covers two distinct roles: the rustic dolt (William here, Audrey, the country characters) and the professional court fool or jester (Touchstone himself). Touchstone is both: he holds the title of court jester and wears 'motley' (the parti-coloured costume of the licensed fool), but he also knows himself to be a wise man among fools. The irony here is that the 'clown' Touchstone enjoys watching is himself a kind of mirror: William is the unwitting version of the wit William lacks.

Touchstone, affecting elaborate courtesy, tells him to put it back on: the comic point is that Touchstone is granting the clown equal social standing, which he is about to strip away the moment he threatens him.

anchor_text: it is a figure in rhetoric that drink, being poured out of cup into a glass
summary: Touchstone constructs a piece of mock-logic: just as pouring drink from a cup into a glass empties the cup, Touchstone's possession of Audrey displaces William's. He bolsters this with a Latin tag — 'ipse is he' (Latin ipse means 'himself,' used in Latin grammar to intensify identity: 'the very man himself') — claiming that because 'all your writers' agree 'ipse is he,' and Touchstone is 'he' who will marry Audrey, William is nobody. The entire argument is gibberish dressed in the costume of formal rhetoric.
detail: The word 'figure' is a technical term from classical rhetoric: a 'figure of speech' or 'figure of thought,' a recognized pattern of argument or expression. Touchstone pretends his cup-and-glass simile is one such authoritative figure. 'Ipse' is a Latin intensive pronoun meaning 'himself/itself'; in schoolroom Latin grammar it was a commonplace of identity ('ipse dixit' — 'he himself said it'). Touchstone appropriates the schoolroom apparatus — 'all your writers do consent' — to overwhelm William with the appearance of learning. The comedy turns on the gap between formal logic's skeleton and the vacuity of the content it clothes, a joke Shakespeare develops more elaborately in Touchstone's mock-treatise on 'the lie' at 5.4.

anchor_text: abandon,--which is in the vulgar, leave,--the society,--which in the boorish is company
summary: Touchstone's dismissal of William is a deliberate parody of the high-flown style of Euphues — the ornate, artificial prose fashion made popular by John Lyly in the 1580s. He translates each hard word into a simpler one mid-sentence: 'abandon' = 'leave,' 'society' = 'company,' 'female' = 'woman.' The joke is that the 'translation' makes the sentence no clearer, since the two halves say the same thing — and the plain version is the one any country fellow could understand without the decoration.
detail: The device is periphrasis (talking around a simple idea with more words) combined with a mock-condescending gloss for each term. 'The vulgar' means ordinary speech, from Latin vulgus (the common people); 'boorish' means rustic or unlettered (from 'boor,' a peasant, from Dutch boer). The parenthetical glosses mimic the style of a pedant explaining Latin to a simpleton, while the effect is the opposite of clarification: Touchstone has delivered a death-threat in three redundant pairs (abandon/leave; society/company; female/woman) so baroque that William barely registers it. The theatrical delight is in the threat's crescendo — 'thou perishest; ... thou diest; ... I kill thee, make thee away, translate thy life into death' — a string of synonyms for a single act, each more direct than the last.

sources.name: OED

anchor_text: in bastinado, or in steel
summary: A bastinado is a beating with a stick or cudgel, specifically on the soles of the feet — a punishment associated with the Ottoman world and with military discipline, but used here as one of Touchstone's comic escalating threats. 'Steel' means a sword or blade. Touchstone is listing his weapons: poison, a stick-beating, or a sword — a comic range from sneaky to clumsy to honorable, none of which he will actually use.

anchor_text: the giddiness of it in question, the poverty
summary: Oliver uses 'giddiness' to mean rashness or foolish levity — the instability of a mind that cannot hold a steady course. The word does not mean physical dizziness here but moral unsteadiness, the quality of someone who acts without due reflection.
detail: The term belongs to the semantic field of 'humours' psychology, in which the well-governed person maintains inner balance and deliberation; 'giddy' and 'giddiness' are standard Elizabethan terms for the inconstancy thought to characterize youth, women, and the lower faculties. Oliver is forestalling Orlando's objection before it is made: he grants that the courtship looks giddy but insists the result — mutual love — justifies it.

anchor_text: my father's house, and all the revenue that was old Sir Rowland's will I estate upon you
summary: Oliver uses 'estate' as a verb meaning to settle or bestow property legally. He is pledging the whole inheritance of Sir Rowland de Bois — the land and income — on Orlando, giving up his own rights as eldest son so he can stay in Arden and marry Celia.
detail: The legal usage is precise: to 'estate' property on someone is to grant a formal legal interest in it, close to the modern 'settle in trust.' An eldest son forfeiting his patrimony was a striking step, but the play has already established Oliver's radical conversion: rescued from a lioness by the brother he had wronged, he is now willing to shed his identity as a great man's heir. The transfer also removes the last material obstacle to Orlando's marriage — his poverty.

anchor_text: Caesar's thrasonical brag of "I came, saw, and overcame"
summary: Rosalind calls Caesar's famous boast 'thrasonical,' meaning vainglorious bragging. 'Thraso' was a stock braggart soldier in the Roman comedies of Terence; his name became the English adjective for military boasting. The famous three-word phrase renders Caesar's report of his lightning victory at Zela in 47 BCE: 'veni, vidi, vici' ('I came, I saw, I conquered').
detail: The Latin formula was reported by Plutarch (Life of Caesar 50) and Suetonius (Divus Julius 37) as Caesar's message conveying the speed of his Pontic campaign; Suetonius records it as displayed at his triumph. The coinage of 'thrasonical' from Thraso, the soldier of Terence's Eunuchus, was so familiar by the 1590s that Touchstone uses the same word to parody it in 5.4. Rosalind deploys both the dramatic allusion and the historical one in the same breath to measure Oliver and Celia's love-at-first-sight against the fastest things in the world: two rams colliding and a conqueror's brag.

anchor_text: in these degrees have they made pair of stairs to marriage, which they will climb incontinent
summary: Rosalind's 'degrees' puns on two senses: the steps of an escalating sequence (met, looked, loved, sighed, sought) and the rungs of a literal staircase leading to the marriage-bed. 'Incontinent' carries a second edge: it means 'immediately' in Elizabethan English but also means 'unable to restrain their desires' — sexual incontinence. Rosalind says they will reach the bedroom with or without waiting for the wedding.
detail: The double meaning of 'incontinent' would have been transparent to the first audience: the word was in regular medical and moral use for lack of self-restraint in bodily appetite, so Rosalind's warning — 'or else be incontinent before marriage' — is a bawdy prediction dressed as a time-reference. The staircase conceit follows the classical and rhetorical device of gradatio (climax), in which each clause adds one step: met, looked, loved, sighed, asked, knew, sought. Shakespeare signals the device and immediately sexualizes it.

anchor_text: how bitter a thing it is to look into happiness through another man's eyes
summary: Orlando's phrase catches the pain of knowing another person is getting the happiness you want. He means both the literal situation — he must watch his brother marry while he remains only in proxy courtship — and the broader condition of desiring what belongs to someone else. The image of looking through another's eyes is exact: joy seen second-hand is diminished and made sour by envy.
detail: The speech is the scene's emotional pivot: it forces Rosalind's hand. Orlando is no longer satisfied with the game of proxy-wooing. He knows his brother will have Celia as a wife tomorrow; by comparison, he has only a youth who pretends to be Rosalind. The rhetoric is Shakespearean antithesis — happiness set against bitterness, the other man's fullness against Orlando's lack — and it directly prompts Rosalind to move toward revelation.

anchor_text: conversed with a magician, most profound in his art and yet not damnable
summary: Rosalind claims she has been trained by a magician who is 'not damnable' — a crucial qualification. Elizabethan law and theology divided magic into lawful 'white' magic (working through natural philosophy and angelic spirits) and unlawful 'black' magic (working with devils), the latter punishable by death and damnation. Claiming a legitimate magician lets Rosalind promise the miraculous without the taint of diabolic bargain.
detail: The 1563 Witchcraft Act made conjuring or invoking evil spirits a felony; the 1604 act under James I extended the penalties. The stage figure of the learned, lawful magician — a 'white' necromancer who controls spirits without selling his soul — was familiar from Marlowe's Doctor Faustus (where Faustus crosses the line) and from the benign magician tradition represented later by Prospero in The Tempest. Shakespeare is careful to have Rosalind say 'not damnable,' which signals to the audience that she is using the white-magic convention as a dramatic convenience, not invoking actual diabolism. In practice the 'magician' is simply herself: she will produce Rosalind by removing her disguise.

anchor_text: It is to be all made of sighs and tears
summary: Silvius delivers a formal catalogue of love's attributes in three stanzas, each followed by a refrain spoken in turn by Phebe, Orlando, and Rosalind. The structure is a litany — a call-and-response prayer form borrowed from church liturgy — applied to secular love. Each speaker's line substitutes his or her own beloved, except Rosalind's, who completes the pattern with 'And so am I for no woman' — a line that is doubly ironic because she is a woman and she does love a man.
detail: The rhetorical device is anaphora (repetition of 'It is to be all made of...') combined with the liturgical litany pattern, a technique that elevates the emotional charge while the escalating series — sighs and tears, faith and service, fantasy, passion, wishes, adoration, duty, observance, humbleness, patience, impatience, purity — builds to a self-parodying excess. The form gently satirizes Petrarchan convention: Silvius is performing love-doctrine rather than feeling it, and the scene's comedy lies in the gap between the solemn form and Rosalind's punchline. The same technique underlies the repeated 'why blame you me to love you' in the subsequent exchange.

anchor_text: And I for Ganymede
summary: Phebe declares love for 'Ganymede,' not knowing that Ganymede is Rosalind in male disguise. In classical myth Ganymede was a beautiful Trojan boy abducted by Jove to serve as cupbearer — and boy-beloved — on Olympus. Rosalind's choice of the name for her disguise loads the scene's four-person love-geometry with a same-sex register: a woman playing a boy named for the most famous divine boy-love, adored by another woman.
detail: On the Elizabethan stage every female role was played by a male actor, so 'Ganymede' is doubly or triply charged depending on how the audience tracks the layers: boy actor plays girl plays boy named for boy-beloved. Phebe's 'And I for Ganymede' places her infatuation in the litany at the same formal level as Silvius's real love and Orlando's real love, dramatizing how the disguise generates genuine, if unresolvable, desire. Shakespeare will untie the knot in 5.4 by revealing Rosalind, at which point Phebe's attraction — technically same-sex — collapses and she accepts Silvius. The Greek myth supplied the Latin word 'catamite' (from Catamitus, the Etruscan form of Ganymede) for a boy used as a sexual partner, so the erotic subtext was available to any educated Elizabethan reader.

anchor_text: howling of Irish wolves against the moon
summary: Rosalind dismisses the lovers' repeated grievances as mindless noise by comparing them to Irish wolves baying at the moon. Ireland was associated in Elizabethan England with uncontrolled wildness, and the wolf — already rare in England by 1600 but still present in Ireland — stood for feral, ungovernable nature. The wolves howling at the moon accomplishes nothing; neither does the lovers' complaint.

The phrase carries a mild ethnic slur of the kind common in Elizabethan writing about Ireland, but its primary force is comic and tonal: Rosalind is losing patience with a situation in which three people are all saying the same helpless thing and nothing changes. The comparison is also precise — wolves howling at the moon is useless noise directed at what cannot hear or respond, exactly as three people saying 'why blame you me to love you' to their respective unreachable objects.

anchor_text: the only pretty ring time
summary: 'Ring time' is spring as the season of betrothal rings and marriage contracts. Rings were exchanged at the formal 'handfasting' — a binding engagement ceremony — that typically took place in spring. anchor_text: These pretty country folks would lie
summary: 'Lie' carries its sexual sense: the country couples make love in the grass margins ('acres') between the strips of rye, the uncultivated headlands left at each end of a medieval ploughed field. The pastoral prettiness of the setting — birds, corn, spring — barely veils what the song describes.

'Lie' meaning to have sexual intercourse is standard Elizabethan usage (OED s.v. 'lie' v.1, sense 14). The joke is central to the song's function: it plays for Touchstone and Audrey, who are about to be married, and for the pair of boy-pages who deliver it to a man old enough to catch every implication. That the song is 'about the fields' is the pastoral-idyll surface; that it is about sex in the fields is what makes it apt pre-wedding entertainment.

anchor_text: the note was very untimeable
summary: Touchstone calls the singing 'untimeable' — a coinage meaning out of musical time, unrhythmic. The pages insist they 'kept time.' Touchstone then twists 'time' from musical measure to time-as-duration: he calls it 'time lost' to hear the song at all. The pun lets him deliver an insult on two levels simultaneously — you were out of rhythm, and you wasted my time.
detail: 'Untimeable' (not otherwise recorded before this passage) is a Shakespearean coinage, built on 'time' as musical beat (OED s.v. 'time' n., sense 14: musical beat or rhythm; 'in time' = in correct tempo). The pages respond to the musical sense — 'we kept time, we lost not our time' — and Touchstone immediately shifts register: 'I count it but time lost' exploits 'time' in its temporal sense (time as a resource squandered) to absorb their defence and redirect it as a second insult. It is characteristic Touchstone: he wins arguments by redefining terms under his opponent's feet, the same move he uses in his degrees-of-the-lie treatise (5.4).

anchor_text: As those that fear they hope, and know they fear
summary: Orlando means: he swings between belief and doubt the way people in a desperate situation both hope for rescue and know they may still be doomed. 'Fear they hope' = are afraid to trust their own hope; 'know they fear' = cannot shake the fear even when they believe. The chiasm (A/B reversed as B/A) enacts the oscillation.
detail: The line is a compressed chiasm: fear/hope :: hope/fear. Orlando has been watching the disguised Rosalind for weeks, half-suspecting the boy's identity, never certain. His suspension of belief is the dramatic problem the Hymen masque will resolve within moments.

anchor_text: the motley-minded gentleman
summary: 'Motley' was the patchwork, multi-coloured cloth worn by professional jesters or fools at court — their distinctive uniform and license to speak freely. Calling Touchstone 'motley-minded' means his mind works the way a fool's costume looks: mixed, incongruous, not committed to one color or view.
detail: The court fool ('licensed fool' or 'clown') wore a particoloured coat as an emblem of his official role: he could say what others could not because his motley declared him harmlessly mad. Jaques coveted a fool's motley and 'liberty' in 2.7 ('I must have liberty / Withal, as large a charter as the wind, / To blow on whom I please'). His delight in Touchstone throughout the play is the delight of a malcontent who lacks the fool's official license for truth-telling. 'Motley' recurs as shorthand for the jester's role from 2.7 ('I am ambitious for a motley coat') through this scene.

anchor_text: let him put me to my purgation
summary: 'Purgation' meant both a medical purge (a laxative or blood-letting that cleared the body) and a legal/ecclesiastical process of clearing oneself of a charge by oath or trial. Touchstone invites any skeptic to 'purge' his credentials as a courtier — either put him through an examination or, in the bodily sense, give him a purge (a joke at his own expense).

Touchstone's humor habitually works by folding the low-bodily into the high-ceremonial.

anchor_text: I have trod a measure; I have flattered a lady; I have been politic with my friend, smooth with mine enemy; I have undone three tailors
summary: Touchstone is cataloguing the marks of a genuine courtier. 'Trod a measure' means danced a stately court dance. 'Been politic with my friend' means plotted shrewdly even with allies. 'Undone three tailors' means ran up unpaid bills — a mark of aristocratic extravagance and contempt for tradesmen.
detail: The 'measure' was a slow, formal court dance (the pavane or similar) requiring accomplished footwork and carriage, a recognized accomplishment of the gentleman. 'Politic with my friend, smooth with mine enemy' captures the court's inverted ethics: treat friends with cold strategy, enemies with flattery. Leaving tailors unpaid was a cliche of the rakish gallant — Thomas Nashe and other satirists make the image familiar. The list is a parody-resume: Touchstone claims every corrupt quality that marks a real court insider.

anchor_text: according as marriage binds and blood breaks
summary: Touchstone says he is here to swear marriage vows and then (presumably) break them, 'according as' — in accordance with the dual reality — marriage creates a formal bond but sexual desire ('blood') strains against it. 'Blood' was the Elizabethan word for carnal passion or lust.

anchor_text: very swift and sententious
summary: 'Sententious' meant full of pithy, morally pointed sayings — packed with 'sentences' (maxims). Duke Senior is praising Touchstone for delivering witty moral aphorisms rapidly, a mark of court eloquence. Today 'sententious' usually implies pompous moralizing, but here it is a compliment.

Erasmus's Adagia and similar collections trained schoolboys to accumulate sentences. The Duke spots the fool doing precisely what the educated were taught to do — packaging wisdom into pointed, swift phrases.

anchor_text: the Retort courteous
summary: Touchstone parodies the elaborate dueling-culture of the Elizabethan and Jacobean gentry, which classified insults and their replies in formal grades. His seven 'degrees of the lie' — Retort Courteous, Quip Modest, Reply Churlish, Reproof Valiant, Countercheck Quarrelsome, Lie Circumstantial, Lie Direct — mock the courtesy-book tradition that tried to codify when a gentleman was honour-bound to fight and when he could let an insult pass without disgrace.
detail: Touchstone's taxonomy mimics the kind of elaborate etiquette guides, such as Vincentio Saviolo's His Practice (1595), that specified exactly which insults obligated a duel. The joke is that an argument about a beard — one of the most trivial possible disputes — has been inflated into a seven-degree system of honour. The crucial exit is the word 'If': 'If I said so, then I said so' converts the Lie Direct into a conditional, which dissolves the obligation to fight. Saviolo's guide and similar Italian fencing-masters' manuals were fashionable in the 1590s; Shakespeare also parodies them in Romeo and Juliet (Mercutio on Tybalt's fencing by 'the book of arithmetic').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2373

anchor_text: we quarrel in print by the book

'in print,' adv.: 'with punctilious exactness') and the literal printed books he is about to invoke ('as you have books for good manners'). Touchstone's joke is that he applies the same pedantic rule-following to a quarrel about a beard as a man of honour would apply to a mortal affront.

anchor_text: much virtue in 'If'
summary: Touchstone's punchline: the word 'If' is the most powerful peacemaker in language, because it converts any direct statement (which demands a response) into a hypothesis (which requires none). The Lie Direct — the most dangerous insult — becomes harmless the moment you phrase it as 'If you said so, then I said so.' Touchstone notes that this tiny word has saved more from duels than all the elaborate degrees of etiquette combined.
detail: The 'much virtue in If' line became a proverbial quotation almost immediately. Its wider implication — that language can always hedge, qualify, and escape commitment — reflects on everything Touchstone says. He is a master of the conditional and the hypothetical throughout the play. It also glances at the theatrical context: drama itself runs on the subjunctive ('if this were a play, if these were lovers...'), so a fool praising the word 'If' is a fool praising theatre.

anchor_text: He uses his folly like a stalking-horse, and under the presentation of that he shoots his wit
summary: A stalking-horse was a real or artificial horse that a hunter hid behind while creeping up on game — the animal screened his approach. Duke Senior says Touchstone deploys his 'folly' (his fool's role) the same way: the apparent foolishness conceals the real shot, which is wit. The best fool-wit lands precisely because it was hidden inside apparent nonsense.
detail: Stalking horses (or, later, canvas cut-outs in horse shape) were standard equipment for wildfowl hunters; the quarry was not frightened because the horse was familiar and unthreatening. The metaphor perfectly captures the Shakespearean licensed fool's method: official license to be an idiot is also license to say true things. Duke Senior, who has been watching Touchstone with delight, gives the play's most direct analysis of how Touchstone's humor works. The 'presentation' (the show or mask of folly) is the screen; the 'wit' is the shot.

anchor_text: Hymen from heaven brought her
summary: Hymen was the classical god of marriage, invoked at Greek and Roman weddings with the cry 'Io Hymen Hymenaee!' and pictured carrying a bridal torch. Bringing a figure representing Hymen on stage — with 'still music' — is a theatrical masque that resolves the play's disguise-plot: the god of marriage himself presents Rosalind and blesses the four couples at once.
detail: The entry of Hymen with 'still music' (soft instrumental music) identifies this as a formal wedding masque, a genre well-established at Elizabethan court entertainments; the mode also appears in The Tempest's betrothal masque (4.1). Catullus's wedding hymns (61-62) use the refrain 'Io Hymen Hymenaee'; Ovid summons Hymen (an ill-omened one) to Orpheus's wedding (Met. 10.1-7). Here the figure is all blessing: the unmasking of Rosalind becomes a sacramental act performed under the god's authority.

Hymen as the classical god of marriage invoked at weddings is standard, the Catullus and Ovid citations are accurate, and identifying the entry with 'still music' as a masque form is defensible — though it should be noted the scene is ambiguous about whether Hymen is a theatrical masque-character or literally divine, a distinction the annotation wisely sidesteps.

anchor_text: Wedding is great Juno's crown
summary: Juno (Greek Hera) was the Roman queen of the gods and the special protector of marriage and women. To call wedding 'Juno's crown' is to identify the institution of marriage as her defining achievement and glory. The song elevates the four simultaneous weddings by linking them to the divine guarantor of matrimony herself.
detail: Juno's role as patroness of marriage (Latin Juno pronuba, Juno who stood beside brides) made her the natural deity to invoke at weddings. In The Tempest 4.1 she presides over the betrothal masque in almost exactly the same capacity. The 'bond of board and bed' (food and the marriage bed) is the standard two-part definition of the conjugal union in canon law: cohabitation and consortium.

Juno as patroness of marriage (Juno pronuba) is accurate classical scholarship, and the parallel with The Tempest 4.1 is a genuine and apt comparison; 'bond of board and bed' as the canonical two-part definition of conjugal union is defensible.

anchor_text: Address'd a mighty power; which were on foot, In his own conduct, purposely to take His brother here, and put him to the sword
summary: 'Address'd a mighty power' means assembled and set in motion a large army. 'In his own conduct' means under his personal command. Jaques de Bois reports that Duke Frederick mobilized troops and led them himself, intending to kill his exiled brother Duke Senior.
detail: 'Address' in Elizabethan English often meant to make ready, prepare, or set in order (OED s.v. 'address' 6: 'to make ready, prepare, array'). 'A power' in military usage is a body of armed men (OED s.v. 'power' 17a). The compressed report is characteristic of late Shakespearean comedy's rapid clearance of plot obstacles — the villain's conversion is described, not dramatized, which keeps the comedy's tone intact.

anchor_text: out of these convertites There is much matter to be heard and learn'd
summary: 'Convertites' are converts — people newly changed in their religious belief or way of life. Jaques means Duke Frederick, who has just converted from worldly ambition to a religious life. The word also glances at Oliver, changed by Orlando's rescue from him. Jaques, the play's perpetual outsider, sees in these sudden conversions material worth studying.
detail: The word carried a double edge: a 'convertite' could be a religious convert, or specifically a reformed sinner (OED, 'convertite' 2: 'a person who has been converted from sin; a penitent'). By leaving to seek out these newly changed people, Jaques remains true to his malcontent character: he prefers the reformed sinner's experience of the world's darkness to the unclouded joy of the weddings. His parting bequests to the others are wry — he gives each exactly what they already have.

anchor_text: thy loving voyage Is but for two months victuall'd
summary: Jaques predicts Touchstone's marriage will dissolve within two months, comparing it to a sea voyage that has taken on only two months' worth of food ('victualled'). When the supplies run out — when the initial desire is satisfied — the voyage (the marriage) will be over. 'Victualled' means provisioned with food.
detail: The voyage metaphor for marriage was conventional, but Jaques gives it a tight cynical timeline. The word 'wrangling' that follows reinforces the comic contract: Touchstone, whose love is appetite rather than devotion, is bound for the port of quarrel, not the haven of long contentment. Jaques's farewell to Touchstone is both accurate and fond — he knows the fool's nature perfectly.

anchor_text: good wine needs no bush
summary: This is a well-known Elizabethan proverb: taverns hung a bush (a bundle of ivy or vine leaves) over their doors as a sign, advertising wine for sale. If the wine was genuinely good, the bush was unnecessary — quality sold itself. Rosalind applies it to the play: a truly good play needs no epilogue to sell it to the audience.
detail: The ivy-bush signboard (Bacchus's plant) was used to identify wine-sellers from Roman times onward and persisted into Elizabethan England. The proverb (Tilley W462: 'Good wine needs no bush') was common enough that Rosalind can assume the audience knows it. Her self-deprecating logic then turns it: since both good wine and good plays do in fact use their 'bushes,' she has grounds to offer an epilogue even to a good play.

anchor_text: my way is to conjure you
summary: 'Conjure' meant both to appeal or entreat solemnly (its ordinary sense here: 'I solemnly charge you') and to use magic spells. Rosalind's epilogue is a playful incantation: she will cast a spell on the women to like the play and on the men to like it in return. The magical frame suits a comedy that has just staged a wedding masque and a goddess.
detail: The word was transitional: 'to conjure' (accent on first syllable) meant to entreat; 'to conjure' (accent on second) meant to practise magic. Shakespeare keeps both active. A professional actor closing a performance would formally appeal to the audience's good will; Rosalind turns it into a theatrical magic — she is, after all, the character who has played magician throughout the wooing plot ('I have since I was three year old conversed with a magician,' 5.2).

anchor_text: If I were a woman, I would kiss as many of you as had beards that pleased me
summary: On Shakespeare's stage, all female roles were played by male actors, usually boys or young men. 'If I were a woman' is therefore both a character's joke (Rosalind, now revealed as a woman, pretends she is not) and the actor's acknowledgment that he is in fact a male performer: the line steps out of the fiction and winks at the theatrical convention.
detail: The line layers four identities simultaneously: (1) Rosalind, a woman in the play's world; (2) Ganymede, her male disguise; (3) the boy actor playing Rosalind and Ganymede; (4) the 'Rosalind' of the epilogue, who speaks as actor-addressing-audience. The 'If I were a woman' formulation is the Epilogue's most precise statement of theatrical self-consciousness: it is true and not-true at the same time, which is what the card on Ganymede explores from the disguise-plot angle. The beards that 'pleased' her echo the beard-quarrel Touchstone has just sent up — a last unexpected echo.

The four-layer identity stack (Rosalind / Ganymede / boy actor / Epilogue speaker) is the mainstream reading of this line and it is clearly supported by the theatrical convention of boy actors — the annotation does not overclaim about Shakespeare's 'intentions,' just describes the layers.
